_doc: T-3645: every evidence note a building's Details tab shows as its "Why" (tools/reading_notes.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the note's own words, since many claims share a note. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the note does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel and camera readings) is left out, so a young reader gets what was read and from where, and what is a guess.

8-10: East of it was Dr. Kimball's home, Bonnell says. He names its use in the same words as the building. It is the one thing about it a record says outright.

Bonnell says Parnick Kelsey used it as a boarding house, said to be run by Eve, his wife. In one line he names the trade, the keeper, and who really ran it. Then he shows the trade was real, because he was turned away with no bed. Two lists of 1843 and 1844 show Kelsey in the same trade years later, on another street.

A book says the Mansion House first stood a little way back from the street. Two years later Mr. Graves built a wood frame part in front, out to the street line. This is the clearest record of a building growing anywhere on this land. A log inn of 1831 stood back from Lake Street. A frame part was built on its front in 1833 and reached the street. Its size is not known, so the two sizes below give our guessed numbers plainly.

The book calls it a barn, and that is our whole reason. A barn is where an animal, a cart or a crop goes in. So its door is wide enough to lead a horse or an ox through. A small door would say it only held things. A wagon door would say a cart went in, and nothing says that. Our guess is only that the old cabin door was made wider.

The old settlers' paper says both bridges stood on ends and two bents. The ends were built of logs in the shallow water near the banks. So the ends stood on log boxes out in the water, not on dry land. That is also why our span, from water's edge to water's edge, is longer than the gap between the ends, by an amount no one recorded.

Andreas says McKee was the government's blacksmith, with his shop near the Agency House. He starts his story of the town's early work with it. No record says who worked here in 1835. McKee carried the mail from 1827. A list from 1830 names him as blacksmith, with Joseph Porthier as his helper. Nothing names a blacksmith here in 1835, so no one is placed here.

His home was a cabin of squared logs, a book says. The same page tells of Harmon's rusty doctor's tools, his hundred books, and his food of flour, bacon and coffee. What it was made of and what it was for are known. When it ended is our guess. Harmon may have been in Texas in 1835, so his own family being here is not sure. The cabin stays put when its owner travels.

Andreas wrote that Beaubien later built a new home and a small trading post. That tells what it was for and that it was small, and nothing more. Small is a word, not a size. So we build the smallest building in the group. No record says what was traded here, so we do not choose.
A book says that in 1831, John Miller built a log house near his brother's inn and used it to tan hides.

A book says there were small log houses near it. The blacksmith, Mr. McKee, lived in one, and Billy Caldwell in one. It names the use and who lived there in one line. Wau-Bun says they were the homes of the men who worked for the government.

The record says that in the back was the large stable and the yard where the wagon trains were driven. There were gates to the yard from both streets. It was one of the most important parts of the inn, for the teams were as many as the guests. Its use is as well known as anything here. The record says it was one of the most important parts. But the building itself is not told of. A known use with an unknown building is the usual state of every back building here.

A book says it was a wood frame building with two floors. The top floor was for school. The lower floor was for church. It cost about nine hundred dollars. Not many old papers tell us the number of floors. This one does.

Newberry and Dole, shipping and trading merchants. That is the firm's own paid ad in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833. It is the first paper of its time we have, and about as good as proof of a trade gets. He paid for it, and his buyers had to find him. A book lists the same firm in the same words. Shipping and trading was the lake trade. They took goods off ships, kept them, and sent them on inland, for a share. The firm's dock got the schooner Illinois, the first ship through the new harbor cut, on 12 July 1834.

Two buildings to let. That is John Wright's own ad in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, offering them until 1 June 1834. Two buildings stood, they were his, and he rented them out. This is one of the two. The ad's end date of 1 June 1834 is not the building's end. A building does not stop when a rental ends. The dates run to the end of 1835.

Cleaver said the ends were built of heavy logs in the shallow water near the banks. He said it in the Tribune in 1893. The same line is in a paper of 1883 that he signed with Caton, Bates and Noble. So it is one man's memory, backed by three more. The ends stood on boxes of logs out in the water, not on dry land. We used to call it the only thing anyone said about how these bridges were built. Then, on 10 August 2026, the rest of that paper was found.

The old settlers' paper says the ends were built of logs in the shallow water near the banks. The bents were four heavy logs. Long heavy logs ran from the ends to the bents. All round or squared logs, not a carpenter's frame. That is what logs means here.

The old settlers' paper says the bents were four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water. We build four heavy logs under a cap at each support, as the line says. Resting on the bottom cannot be seen here. We do not build the river bed, or anything more than half a meter under the water. So a support standing on the bottom and one pounded into it look the same above water. That part lives in this note, as it does for the North Branch bridge.

One record says the lighthouse was forty feet high, with four mirrors to send out the light, in a lantern room like a bird cage. Andreas, more careful, says it had one mirror. We do not build the mirrors. We build a glass room at the top, which both records agree on.

A book says a log house used to tan hides, Chicago's first known factory. Another says he ran a tannery just north of Miller's inn. Its use is the best known thing about it, but the model cannot show it. What stands is a log house, because that is what was built, and the yard that made it a tannery is not built. If it was still tanning on 1 July 1835 is not known. The partner came in 1832, and then the trade drops out of the record. So this tells what the building was for, not what it was doing that day.

A log house. That is the one thing any record says about its walls. We build it of cut logs with notched corners. Whether the logs were cut or round, and how the gaps, roof and floor were done, are not known.

A book says a meat plant was built on the South Branch, where about three hundred cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed that year. The building and its first season are all that is known. July is between packing seasons, which are in winter. So on the day we show, the plant is standing, but not working.
A book calls it a frame building of two floors. People who stayed there talk about the second floor again and again. One said a stairway in the hall went up to the second floor.

A book says they added a house of two floors to the cabin, facing the river. The 1833 picture shows a building of two floors next to a log cabin, from the south bank. That is the number of floors the records give. It used to sit in the wrong place in our record, and went to the log part by mistake.

A book says he built a log house near his brother's inn and used it to tan hides. Another book calls it a tannery but does not say what it was made of. So the logs rest on one record. They fit everything else at the forks in 1831.

It cost about nine hundred dollars. That is not a thing to build, but it is the only number we have about its size. The shape above comes from it, using what the two churches cost for their size. If a real size is ever found, this number is what was wrong about the math, not the other way round.

A book lists a soap and candle works run by Daniel Elston and partners. The ad itself, from 26 November 1833, offers cash for tallow and for ashes. The tallow is the interesting part. Tallow is fat left over from killing animals, and we build those butcher houses too. A town that killed 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs in a season had the fat for a candle works. That is why we felt we could place this record at all. It links two trades, not two known businesses.

A book calls it Clybourne's first log butcher house, built in 1827. A few pages later it calls it his log butcher house on the east side of the North Branch. Two lines, the same word. This is the best-known fact about the building.

A website says it was the stopping place for all the farmers coming to town from the west. It took in farmers and wagon drivers, who were the travelers then. It was the west side's inn for the wagon trade. Its guests were not like those of the Green Tree a block north, or the Sauganash across the river. The website also calls it one of the best hotels in town.
Our guess. 1.35 meters wide, wide enough to push a barrow of bark through, and narrower than a wagon door. It fits in the 2.44 meter wall with a post on each side.

Our guess. 12 tents, and not a count of anyone. 77 visitors at the land sale had no bed. At four men to a tent, they would fill this many tents and more. Most slept in rooms and on floors. Twelve tents is our share for those who came with tents.

A fix to a mistake people repeat. Some say the Green Tree was whitewashed, even our own notes. But the whitewash was inside. Edwin Gale wrote that the walls and ceilings inside had been whitewashed when it was built. Nothing tells of the outside. We use bare gray boards. In 1831, people wrote of the white paint on the Sauganash as something special. That fits. A photo from about 1859 would settle it.

No chimney. Zero is a claim too. Nothing is known about heat here. A store house for barrels and hides is the one kind of building here with no reason for a fire. The killing that needed fire was done in a yard, not inside. If the building was also an office, it had a stove, and this is wrong by one.
No chimney is a claim, not a gap. A food store is the one building in a fort where you do not want a fire. Nothing tells of a chimney on it. So we say none, and build none.
No chimney. Zero is a claim too. A gun shed had no heat, so it has no chimney.

A freight shed held goods, not people, and whose goods they were is not known. The building and its use come from a picture the owner gave us on 18 August 2026. It draws low store houses on the banks below the Dearborn bridge. This stretch is where the river traffic and the town's one bridge over the main river met in July 1835. No record names a shipper or keeper for any of these sheds. A firm written in here would be made up. A family placed in it would be made up people sleeping in a shed. So the roof says its use and what is missing, and no one is placed in it. A record naming the store houses here would give it a keeper.

A garden's dates are its fort's. It is drawn and named on the 1830 plan, and in 1831 someone walking by saw it full of fruit. So it was there on both sides of 1835. We end it when the soldiers left on 29 December 1836, not when the buildings were torn down. Soldiers kept the garden, and after that date there were none. Nothing tells what happened to it.

A no, written down so no one adds one by guessing. The church had no tower. St. Mary's has the same trap: it got a low tower some time later, and building it would make that church look newer than 1835. We say so here because people expect a church to have a tower.
Four wagons in a group, our guess. In 1835, some families came to Chicago by land, from Indiana and Ohio. Others came by lake. A group went on the road together.

A price proves a service. The building is our guess. On 13 April 1831 the county set the prices tavern keepers could charge. Feeding a horse was 25 cents, and keeping a horse one night was 50 cents. We take that to cover every inn here. That is a guess, since we have not read this hotel's own license. It does not prove a stable. A horse can be tied to a rope, kept in a fenced lot, or kept up the street. We build a stable because a hotel this size, on a lot with an alley, usually had one.

A square about 53 meters on a side. That it was square comes from a book on the rebuilt fort, and the 1830 plan agrees. The size is worked out, not written. No record gives its size. So 53 meters is measured from the 1830 plan, and it could be off by a fifth. The fort was somewhere from 140 to 210 feet on a side. We build a box because the plan draws one. Nothing says its corners were square or its sides exactly equal.

A blacksmith shop from October 1833, doing the iron work the town and the road trade needed. A book says Temple and Co. asked him to do the iron work for the first coach line between Chicago and St Louis in January 1834. From the spring of 1834 he made the old Bull plow, with a wood blade. That plow is why this building matters beyond its corner. It was the tool for wet prairie. A blacksmith on the west side making plows is the farm land around the town coming into the town. If he was making them on 1 July 1835 is not known.

A building site in July 1835, not the finished hotel. A notice in the Chicago Democrat of 10 June says a house was being built in Kinzie's Addition. It is thought to be the Lake House. No record measures how far the work was in July. Thick brick walls step down from a higher front to a lower back. Some openings for windows are cut, and only a few have wood across the top. A wide gap at the back lets in supplies. Two short wood platforms stand inside for the builders. All of these are our guesses for a working site, not taken from the later picture. Piles of brick, wood and stone stand in the yard. No digging or basement is shown.
A small home for a man who made bricks. It is next to Blodgett's yard, where bricks were made. We build that too.
A carpenter's own house on the north side. Maybe he built it better than the ones he built for others. But nothing says so. We claim only a plain cottage.
This follows from the open side. You can push a cart straight in, so no door is needed. Cutting one would mean a wall that we do not build.

The wall is 3.35 meters to the roof edge. That shows about 0.9 meters of log wall above the fence of posts, as both later pictures show a big log block above the fence. Our old height hid almost all the wall. Neither picture gives a measure. The exact height, and that it was so in July 1835, are our guesses.

Our guess, like the building. Goods go in and out of a freight shed by cart. So it gets a wagon door, not a door for people. Our list says wide doors for this kind too. It opens on the yard between the two sheds. The yard is big enough for a wagon to stand at either door. It is reached from the east end of South Water Street.
Our guess, like the building. Goods go in and out of a freight shed by cart. So it gets a wagon door, not a door for people. Our list says wide doors for this kind too.

A store that sold many things. The ad of 18 November 1833 lists cloth, dishes, tools, food and drink. It also sells a big lot of leather and saddles for others. That makes it a shop that sold goods for others too, like most of South Water Street.
A food store on the way in from the west side. The keeper lived in rooms behind it and above it. That is the most common small shop building in a town this size.
A harness maker's shop on the edge of town. It made harness for work horses. It is not the known saddle shop of Goss and Cobb.
A worker's shack of boards on the west edge of town. Few lots are built there, and the cheapest roofs stand.
A worker's shack on the edge of the north side.
A light color in a black and white picture does not tell the color or what was on it. Whitewash is our guess.
A tower with a light for ships. It was the first one built on the lake.
A meat shop in the town. A town of 3,265 people would not walk three kilometers up the river to Clybourne's to get meat for dinner.

A thing it did not have. A book says the church itself was not plastered. That sets it apart from the Presbyterian church, whose walls were plastered. It is the clearest sign of how rough St Mary's was in 1835. We do not build the insides of buildings anyway.

A bridge for everyone, and the first bridge in Chicago that could open. A book says the first drawbridge on the river was at Dearborn Street. Before it, the town ran a free ferry here. It was a flat boat pulled on a rope. When the bridge opened, the ferry moved to Rush Street. The bridge was the only fixed way between the north and south sides of town. By 1835 it was even an address. A new paper set up its office in June 1835 on Water Street, near the drawbridge.

A public crossing, and the town's first bridge of any kind. It took the place of the Miller ferry, which had crossed the same water between Miller's house and the Wolf Point inn since 1829. By 1835 it joins the west side's Canal Street to the north bank.
A ring around the fires. One group camps around its own fires, with its wagons drawn up close.
A root house has no heat. That kind of building never does.
The tents are spread out, not in a row. People came in groups over two weeks, and each set up where there was room.
The tents are spread out, not in a row. Families came off boats over two weeks, and each set up where there was room.
A second barrel maker, next to the Newberry and Dole meat plant on the South Branch. Barrels were made where the packing was done. We build the plant too.
A second worker's shack on the same edge of town.
A shoemaker's shop on Lake Street. It is one of six small craft shops in our plans.
A blacksmith on the west side, on the road. That is where a smith who lives off passing horses and wagons wants to be. We say the same for Pierce's shop one block north.
A pole has no roof. We keep this item because our builder reads it.

A store selling food and goods for trade with the Native people, a website says. A book lists its keeper among the town's traders with the Native people, and among those allowed to sell goods. What it sold on 1 July 1835 is not known. There is a reason to doubt it went on. The 1833 Treaty of Chicago gave up the land, and the Native people were being moved west all through the summer of 1835. So the trade with them was ending as the scene opens. We build a store standing, and claim nothing about what was on its shelves.

A street crossing over a backwater, and the least of the three. Here is what makes it stand out. It is the only thing built on the north side's river front to deal with the ground. The north side's river street is cut in two by a wet ditch, two hundred meters from the forks. Either the town got across it, or the street stopped.

A street crossing over a stream. It is here only because the ground under South Water Street is water. It is not a river bridge. No one was proud of it, and unlike the other crossing, no one wrote it down. It belongs in the scene because the ditch does. A street that meets a six meter stream must cross it or stop. The town's 1833 order says South Water did not stop.

A street crossing over a stream. It is not a river bridge, and no one was proud of it. What makes it stand out is what it says about the ground. The south side's main stream ran through the middle of town, across its busiest street. For at least seven years, the town's answer was some logs. It belongs in the scene for the same reason the mud does.
A tailor's shop on the same street. It is smaller, as a trade making clothes to order would be.
A stable for a wagon driver on Canal Street, where the country roads come into town. The Western Hotel keeps its own wagon yard there too.

A warehouse had no shop window. A book tells of a warehouse and a yard for killing animals. Goods went in and out by cart. No one was served at a counter. So we turned off our usual shop front on purpose. That is a guess from how it was used.

A wash house on the north side, with a big pot, a fire and a yard to dry clothes. It washed for the boarding houses on the same ground. We know this work went on because the inns were so crowded. But no record names it.
A wheel maker's shop next to the blacksmith. The two trades worked on the same wagons, and in 1835 they stood next door.
A box 1.2 meters square, about an eighth of the roof's width. That is big enough to look like a small air vent on a barn, without taking over the 47-foot barn. The exact width is a guess.

An ad proves a trade, not a building. Our own record warns of that, about the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833. We know Daniel Elston and partners made soap and candles in Chicago that November. They paid cash for tallow, which is animal fat, and for ashes from people's homes. A book lists the same business. We start in November 1833 because that is the ad's date. The works were already running then. That it lasted to July 1835 is a guess, and our confidence says so. Nothing follows the business after that ad. Elston shows up again years later, as a town leader and running the biggest brickyard by 1854. A long life in town hints he did not fail in 1834. That is not proof about a building. The record ends at the end of 1835.

Known for 1850, and carried back. Fergus tells of a square post, 8 inches wide, set in the ground, about 2 feet high. On top was a brass plate that had been a sundial. Both sizes here are his. The date is the weak part. He saw something old in 1850. Nothing puts it here in 1835. But a fort with soldiers needs a sundial more than an empty one. Where it stands is our guess. We put it in the south part of the open ground.

About 10 and a half feet, taller than our usual for this size. This building has a reason. Barrels are closed standing up and piled two high. A 3 meter wall with a beam across would not clear them. The range is reasoned. The number inside it is our guess.

About 77 meters on a side, some 250 feet square, a little more than an acre and a half. Measured from the 1830 plan. That fits gardens for two groups of soldiers. It is the biggest fenced space we have drawn. The plan draws it as a diamond with sides not quite equal. We made it square, which moves the corners a few meters.
About a wagon wide. It is our guess, since there is nothing about this crossing to work from. See the note on its shape for why it is the smallest of the three.

People came into an auction room. Goods were called out inside to a crowd, not shown in a window to the street. Andreas tells what the room was for, but not what its front looked like. So we chose a front with no shop window. That is a guess from how it was used.

A stray is a lost farm animal. A stray pen held it until its owner came for it. That was a job for the town, so a book calls this the town's first public building. For its first months it held prisoners too, for want of anything better. That is why the log jail was built later.
One of the made-up buildings that fill the town for July 1835. It is not proof this building stood.

Andreas calls the building a house. He also says Madore Beaubien got a license to sell goods in 1831, the year it was built. So the shop half is our guess, from the dates and from where it stands on the main street. No record says goods were sold in it. What it was used for on 1 July 1835 is not known at all.

A book dates the warehouse and the yard for killing animals to 1832, with no month, so we start at the beginning of that year. That it still stood in 1835 is a guess, and there is a reason to doubt it. In 1834 Newberry and Dole built a butcher house on the South Branch. A butcher trade moves there when it outgrows a yard behind a store. So the yard had likely moved by 1835. The warehouse is another matter. Nothing follows it, so we keep it. Note: their other warehouse, where a ship was cheered in July 1834, was on the north side of the river. This is a different one, on the south side. Do not mix them up.
A book dates the warehouse and the killing yard to 1832.
A book says the summer of 1832. Charles Cleaver, remembering in 1893, says the winter of 1831 to 1832.

A book says two named owners opened it to the public and ran it for four years. That is a public house. The American tells what kind in June 1835. A dentist could take its rooms for a season, and a doctor could give it as his work address. That is how a town hotel was used in 1835. So we call it an inn, not just a bar.
Andreas lists it as part of the home: a new house and a small trading post. That ties it to the home. What it traded, and who ran it in 1835, are not claimed.

Andreas says Bates built it and ran the auctions. From 1833 Bates also helped at the post office, sorting mail in Hogan's store at the other end of the street. In the model the two buildings are 570 meters apart, and the same man worked in both.

A book names Clybourne as the builder in 1827, and as the one who ran it in 1833. Dole packed meat here that year too. No record says if anyone worked here on 1 July 1835. Packing was winter work, so in July it was most likely a building standing empty between seasons.

A book names the trade plainly. Kimball was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street. The trade is the best known thing about this record. That is the other way round from most buildings here.
A book says J. H. Kinzie put ads in the paper in 1834 as a shipper. It also lists a Kinzie store on South Water Street by 1833. The trade is known. Which building it was in is not.

A book says frame, and no more. The word does not tell which of the two kinds of frame. The light kind was first used in Chicago in 1832 and 1833, and soon became the usual one. This building's date is not fixed, and may be before that. So the older kind is the safer guess. If the store went up in 1833, it could just as well have been the light kind. Nothing settles it.

Andreas says it was wooden, and that is all. We build it with a sawn wood frame, not logs. A frame holds up one big open room, and logs do not. New stores in town in 1833 and 1834 were going up in frame. The records never say which kind of frame.
Andreas tells the paper's name, who started it, when, how big it was, and where its office was. We know the office was there. That it had a building of its own is not known.

Andreas wrote one line. He says small log houses near the agency were lived in by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and by Billy Caldwell. Caldwell was a chief and a speaker of languages for the agency. We know the two men lived here. We do not know which man had which house.

A book tells of the town a visitor saw in the 1830s. It says there was not one church tower, nor a chimney four feet above a roof. A flagpole at the fort, about fifty feet high, flew a worn flag in fair weather and on holidays. Coming from the south, the same book says, you saw a line of hard-to-make-out buildings, and the flag over the fort, if it was flying. This is the second fort. It is the book's own story of the years around 1835.

A book says the rebuilt fort had strong corners at the north-west and south-east, and the blockhouse in the south-west. Kinzie says strong corners at every other corner. Hubbard says in 1827 the blockhouse was at the south-west and a strong corner at the north-west. The 1830 plan draws one at three corners and leaves the north-east plain. Many say there were two blockhouses, at the south-east and north-west. That was the first fort, before 1812, not this one. It is the most common mistake about it.
A book says Mr. Jackson built one more tower, forty feet high, in 1832.
A book tells of it. In 1834, Oliver Newberry and George Dole had a plant built on the South Branch. It was a place to kill and pack meat.

A book says it was made of long logs laid across. Cleaver says the ends were built of heavy logs. Two records, both telling of round or squared logs, not a carpenter's frame. That is what logs means here.
A book says the Mansion House was built in 1831 by Dexter Graves. The frame front in this scene was added two years later.

Andreas calls it a log house of two rooms. No record tells how the corners or gaps were done, or if it had boards on it. We build squared logs, the most common kind in Chicago in 1831, and what the record says.
A book calls it the first log butcher house, built by the owner in 1827.
A book tells us when it began. Asahel Pierce began to build a blacksmith shop on 8 October 1833.
A book says Carpenter built a small store in the summer of 1833.

A book says Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street and built a small store in the summer of 1833. No month is given, so we start it on 1 August, the middle of summer. He moved into this store, so it likely still stood in 1835. His ad in a paper in November 1833 sold drugs, paints, food, glass and nails. That shows him at work three months later. The ad has no address, so it could be from his other shop. The end date is just where our record stops.
A book says Mark built one more house on the corner of Wells and Lake in 1834.
A book says a log building. No record tells how the corners or gaps were done, or if it had boards on it. We build squared logs, the most common kind at the forks in 1832, and what the record says.
A book says it was a wood frame store of two floors. The unfinished loft above them is counted on its own, not here. The number of floors counts only the finished floors.
One of the 665 made-up roofs that fill the town for July 1835. Nothing proves this building stood, and no record names anyone on this lot.
One of the made-up roofs that fill the town for July 1835. Nothing proves this building stood.
Juliette Kinzie saw it in 1831, and no one else ever did. It starts with the fort. It ends when the soldiers left for good, since soldiers kept a root house. Nothing follows it after that.

A book says so twice, with dates on both sides of July 1835. It says the Murphys took over the new hotel in August 1834 and stayed until 1836. Then they moved to the old Sauganash. So July 1835 falls in their time, with eleven months on each side. That makes this the best-known stay in this part of town. One record does not agree. Our notes link Abram A. Markle to the house in 1835 and 1836, and an 1836 ad calls it Markle's Exchange Coffee House. But the book says Markle ran a different hotel in 1835. Either he ran both, or one date is loose. We keep the Murphys, since their dates are on both sides.

Built in the spring of 1835, before the day we show. A book says he built a house on what he thought was his lot. Then he found he was on Monroe Street, not Adams. So he moved it there on rollers. The house, the season, its owner, and that it was moved a block are all known. The dates start on 1 March 1835, the earliest spring could be.
Bare brick. Nothing says it was painted or whitewashed. The whitewash in the old records is on a board fence of the 1850s. It is also in one man's memory of the first fort.
Records show that Beaubien used the cabin as a barn. He lived at this home from 1817 to about 1840. No one lived in a barn, so this tells whose farm building it was.

A book of 1902 puts John Beach in a house partly inside the jail yard, facing Randolph Street, in a walk set in 1835. But its picture says 1836. The dates are our usual limits, not when it was built or torn down. They do not prove every part of the picture was there by 1 July 1835.

Both of its uses are known, each on its own. The store: Peck had a license to sell, and put ads in the paper for cloth, tools and food in 1834 and 1835. The home: a book says Peck lived at the store. The loft above the two floors was let to a guest at least once, to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter in May 1833.

Both men are named for starting the yard in the spring of 1833. No record says if either still worked here on 1 July 1835. Andreas says Daniel Elston ran the biggest of the city's five brickyards by 1854. That is twenty years later and tells us nothing about 1835.
Both pictures show the keeper's house with a roof of two slopes. Which way it faces is not the same in the two drawings.

Both ads are signed John Holbrook, at Chicago, on 10 and 13 June 1835. That he traded, what he sold, and his street and corner are all known. His building, its size and height, and how far his door was from the corner are our guesses.

Both records say it was made of logs. In 1838 the church group moved it. They floated the cabin across the river and rolled it on logs. That only works for a log house that is light and strong enough to move in one piece.

Both records say Stow built the house and ran it. The list of hotels says it plainly: built and run by W. H. Stow. He came to Chicago about 1833, so he was here on the day we show, whichever year it was built.

Both records name Davis as the keeper in 1835. A book's list of people who put ads in the Chicago American in its first year has John Davis, Steamboat Hotel. But that is the year, not the day. A website says J. Dorsey and J. Force took over running it on 9 November 1835. So Davis ran it on the day we show, if it was open at all. A Mr. Davis also took over the Sauganash in 1835. If that was the same John Davis is not known, and we do not guess.

Both records say it had two uses. They do not agree on which came first. A website says Walker built it for a place to pray, and for a school house. Wau-Bun says it was first meant for a school house, but used now and then for church, when a traveling minister came by. Either way, on 1 July 1835 it is the only building here put up for church or school. Jesse Walker himself died in 1835.

Braunhold's print draws the two front windows bare, with log wall next to their frames, and no open shutters. The main hotel's shutters in a later copy belong to a different building, and do not mean this cabin had them. This is for the front only. Nothing is claimed about the back.

Braunhold made an old print of the Sauganash for a book of 1884. It shows this log cabin joined to it. The cabin has one door between two tall windows. The tops of the windows are about level with the top of the door. Which cabin it is comes from a caption we already use, not a new record. The windows are set evenly along the front, as before. That is our guess, not measured from the picture.

Braunhold's print of 1884 draws one chimney on this log cabin. A caption we already use says the cabin was Carpenter's old shop. We used to guess one chimney only because it needed heat in winter. Now the picture shows it. That it comes up through the roof is from the picture. Its exact place and size are our guess. The print's brick and another artist's red do not match our chimney's stick and clay, and we do not claim they do.

It was built to kill cattle for the soldiers at the fort. From 1833 it packed meat to sell. That year the owner packed about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs. A man named Dole packed 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs here too. The book gives the prices. This was the first butcher house in Chicago. The city later grew big on this trade. The book also calls the owner the government's butcher for the Potawatomi. A treaty set up that job. That is what the man was, so we keep it. We mark it to be checked, like the rest of this record's Native history.

Built in 1833 by James Kinzie, the first building in town made to be an inn. It stood at the corner of Lake and Canal until 1880. Then it was moved to Milwaukee Avenue, to make room for a big iron works. Both dates are known. But the building grew in that time. John Gray ran it from 1838 to 1841. He remembered a low one-floor room added on the right, the same as on the left. No one dates those rooms. Two pages of one website give 1880 and 1881 for the move. That does not matter for 1835. Who built it is mixed up too. One page says Philo Cobb. A book says Silas Cobb, a real man, and is almost for sure right.
Built in 1834. Nelson R. Norton began it in March 1834, and a book says the town took it that summer.

Caton's attic is the point. It is the only record here of what a newcomer with schooling did for money, and where he slept, in the town's first summer. It makes this building a place to sleep as well as an office. That is the mixed use our plans have for this kind of building.

Fixed on 10 August 2026. We had picked wrong between two readings. The record that settles it was signed by the man the losing side leaned on. The old settlers' paper of 1883, signed by Caton, Bates, Cleaver and Noble, says both bridges stood on ends and two bents. It says the bents were four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water. So bent is the settlers' own word. We now build four heavy logs under a cap at each support. Resting on the bottom cannot be seen here, since we do not build the river bed. So that part lives in this note. Our old reason was that Cleaver told of logs in shallow water, like a box of logs. A modern table called it a bent, and we trusted the man who saw it over the table. We also guessed the middle supports were built like the ends. That is what the 1883 paper overturned: someone did tell of the middle.

Cameron shows a dark, open door with a person in it. We build a dark, open door. Nothing is known about the inside, the door itself, who the person was, or if the door was open in July 1835. It follows the picture of 1833, made years later.
Cameron shows a dark top that sticks out on the short chimney. So we build a cap on it. Its size and color are our guess, since the picture is black and white.

In Cameron's picture the pointed end has a small box above the log wall. Its size and place are our guess. We build it as a wood hatch, not a glass window. The painting does not show if it was glass or boards. We do not guess that anyone slept up there.
Records show that Chappel lived here in 1833 and 1834, and left before 1835. No record names anyone here in 1835. So we give his stay its end date, and do not carry him into 1835. That is on purpose.

This was Chicago's first brickyard. Tyler K. Blodgett started it in the spring of 1833, with Henry S. Lampman as his worker. Andreas calls Lampman the first brick-maker here. He says the yard made the bricks for the first brick building in Chicago. That was Blodgett's own house, across the river from the yard. It was 20 feet square, with one and a half floors. That house is not built in the model yet.
Long boards that overlap hide the frame. The kind of frame is our usual, not seen.

We know what it was made of, what it was for, who ran it and where it stood. Andreas tells of a log house run as a fine boarding house by Mrs. Rufus Brown. It was the first building behind Peck's store, at South Water and LaSalle. We start it at the beginning of 1833. That is not when it was built. It is when we know it stood and took in boarders. No record follows it past 1835.

Known, which is rare here. A book says the outside of the building was not painted, and it had no steeple or tower. It is the only outside finish told of on any building on this land. It backs our guess for the Green Tree and the Presbyterian church: bare gray boards were the usual. The Sauganash's white paint was the one worth writing about. The line about no tower is from when it was built in 1833, not 1835. The bell tower we build is our guess.
Dark shutters stand open at the windows in the picture. The black and white picture does not show their color. Green is our guess.
A box of about 10.3 by 19.7 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 10.4 by 18.9 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 10.5 by 19.4 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 11.6 by 20.3 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 6 by 8.8 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 6 by 14.6 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 6.2 by 9.8 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 6.7 by 14 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 6.9 by 13.4 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.
A box of about 9.6 by 17.3 meters, picked from our list of sizes for this kind. No sizes are known for this made-up building.

Known, but not a thing to build. We do not build insides. Splitting the floors left no sign outside that we build, no outside stair and no different windows above. It is recorded because it is the whole point of the building, and it is what ties Sproat's school to this place.

Known, but not built. The benches are the clearest fact about the inside. They also check the size: 1,000 square feet for 200 people is 5 square feet each. That is tight, but it is what bench seats give. We do not build insides, so they can't be seen.

Known, but not built. These two go together because they tell about money. The walls were finished but the floor was not. That is what a $600 church paid for by its members looks like inside. St. Mary's had no plaster at all. We do not build insides, so neither can be seen.
Known, but not built. It is the most lively known fact about the inside of the building. We do not build insides, so none of it is shown.

Known, but not built. This is the only thing any record says about the inside. The schoolroom and the teacher's rooms were under one roof. We do not build the insides of buildings, so the wall between them can't be seen. But it is why the house is sized for two rooms, not one.

Known twice, once from its own time. The ad in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 says it was a food store. A book says the same, with a shipping trade added by 1834. The trade is the best known thing about it.

The flag hangs on its own pole on the roof. The pole is 4.25 meters tall, our guess. From the picture, the flag is about 1.85 meters long and 1.3 meters tall. Those sizes are our guess too, since a picture with depth and folds cannot give meters. If the date or the pole does not match, the flag is not shown. That keeps the 24 star flag from showing in later years without a check.

Flown because the owner asked, as our guess. The book says the flag flew in fair weather and on holidays. Wednesday 1 July 1835 was not a holiday, and no record tells the weather. The scene is drawn on a fair summer day, so the flag is up, as the book's rule allows. No record says so. The breeze that holds it out is our guess too.

Four is our number. What the record gives is the load. The 1883 paper calls both river bridges wagon bridges, with long heavy logs from end to bent and bent to bent. The parade of 18 August 1835 crossed this one. A deck carrying wagons over three spans of 18.7 meters needs more than the two logs of a footbridge. So four under a full deck is the strong reading. But the number is no one's. A record that said three or five would take its place, and change nothing else here. This one was called a wagon bridge from the start.

Every number is our guess. Four rooms and a kitchen are known. No size is. We read it as the most common way to get four rooms under one roof in a wood house of 1834. A front part of 24 by 18 feet with a floor and a half: two rooms below, and two bedrooms under the roof. The kitchen is a 12 by 14 foot wing at the back. The ad says with a kitchen attached. We read it as a wing, not a cook house on its own. The ad names the barn and garden in the same line, and those were clearly apart. A kitchen on its own is the other fair reading. It would change the plan, not the count. The whole is 24 by 32 feet, inside our sizes.

Four rooms is the proof. Two below and two under the roof keeps the house in the town's most common kind. One floor with four rooms is the other choice. That would be a bigger building for the same number of rooms.

Frame is known, but the kind of frame is not. So the grade follows the weaker half. The record says a frame building of two floors, and no more. We pick the older kind of frame, as for the Sauganash. The records never use a word that tells the two kinds apart. This building's date falls in just the years when the light frame was taking over in Chicago. If the date turns out to be 1835, not 1833, the light frame is the better guess.

Fergus, writing in 1850, names the building where the cannons were kept. He gives no other name. A warning: the line about three small cannon is about the first fort, before 1812. Nothing says what guns were at this fort in 1835. No gun is built.

Five windows and one door at the end, to match the long wall in Moss's old print, which has no date. Using them for 1835 is our guess, not a known list of openings in 1835. The window size and panes are our guess too. The picture is not treated as a measure.

Four chimneys with caps can be seen in the picture. Their exact places and heights, and which side of the roof each one comes through, are our guess. Using this picture, which has no date and was made years later, for 1835 is our guess too.

Fourteen feet, and our guess. See the note on its shape for the math. Eight feet for wagons and six feet of boards for people to walk, because the owner asked for a crossing for the road and for the sidewalk. This is the narrowest that carries both. It does not mean this crossing was finer than the town's main bridges. It is one wagon and one path wide, as asked.

Frame is known. The kind of frame is not. The light kind was first used in Chicago in 1832 and 1833. By the time this building went up, it was the usual one here. So it is the better guess for 1834. That is the opposite of the Sauganash of 1831, where the same reason gives the older kind. It cannot be seen from outside. We record it so our two frame inns do not quietly get the same answer for different reasons.

A roof of two slopes is our guess, from its kind and from Moss's old print, which has no date. We used to say it had no steeple in 1835. But the book says it had none when it was built in 1833. The bell tower we build now is our guess, since no one knows when it was added. The roof's shape, the building's size and its wall height stay the same.

A book of 1902 says the first Tremont was yellow, in a walk set in 1835. We keep the three floors and shutters from the picture, and take only the yellow color from the book. Gifford's black and white drawing shows no color. The exact yellow and trim colors are our guess. The book's smaller size with two floors is kept as another version, not as an earlier stage.

Long outer braces, a test. The 1884 picture shows long braces on the outside, fixed high on the tall posts. Before, ours were fixed only 2.6 meters above the bridge floor. Now they are fixed at 5.2 meters, below the top of the frame. That tests what the picture shows. The other sizes are our guess, not measured.

Side walls of boards laid flat. A picture printed in a book in 1884 shows wide side walls with flat boards along the bridge. That picture was drawn later, so using it for 1835 is a guess. The height of the side wall stays at 0.95 meters, with posts about 2.2 meters apart. The sizes of the boards and caps are our guess. Nothing else on the bridge changes. We do not claim a match.

How tall the tall frames over the bridge stood is the biggest thing we can see but do not know. No record gives their height, shape or ropes. We know they were tall enough to look scary at night, and strong enough to hold the sixty-foot bridge part up for two days. 6.4 meters, about 21 feet, is our usual number. It makes a frame look like a lifting frame, not a gate post. It is not a finding. We build them anyway, see-through in the confidence view, to say this shape is ours. Leaving them out would say the bridge was just a plain road over the water, and that would be more wrong. Plans from 1834, or any old picture of the river mouth, could settle it.

Hubbard says the trading house had two floors. We say the two floors are block A's, and that is our guess. Hubbard names one building, a two-floor house of squared logs. The plan writes that name over three blocks. So which block it is, is not on the map. We pick A for two reasons. The label starts just past A's corner and touches no other block. And A is the only one big enough for a home and store with two floors. Neither reason is proof. The other way would have put one floor here on no proof at all, while a man who saw it said two. Taking his word, and saying how far we had to carry it, is the better answer.

Hubbard's one word is all we have, and it does not say what it was made of. He calls them rough wash houses. That says rough, but not rough in what. We build it of boards nailed up and down, with gaps between. That is our idea of a rough work building put up fast for wet work. We pick it over logs for one reason. A wash house wants air and light through its walls, and a log building gives neither. That is our reason. No one wrote it down.

The flag pole rises 4.25 meters above the roof top, a size that fits how it looks. It stands a bit over a third of the way along the roof. The picture has no scale. None of the spots we picked on it give meters or a place on the ground.
Cameron's picture shows rows across the pointed end, around the small box. So that end is built in rows, not smooth. The picture does not show if they were logs or boards. Their sizes are our guess.
Hubbard says in 1827 that the fort's leaders lived in it. A list from 1855 calls it the leader's house. A book says the officers had rooms inside the fort's walls.

Hubbard calls it the military barn. The 1830 plan draws the Big Barn with Cupola inside the fort's fence, by the fort's field. Soldiers were here all the way from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 its work buildings were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

Hubbard calls it the military barn, in those words. The plan calls it the Big Barn with Cupola and draws it inside the fort's fence, next to the field that belonged to the fort. What was kept in it is not known, and we do not guess. A fort's barn held hay, horses and farm tools, but which of those is a guess. The record claims the building, not what was in it.

Hubbard names the fort's store in 1827, and the 1855 list names it too. There is another answer, and it is not settled. In 1850 Robert Fergus told of a building just east of the blockhouse. He said it was the rooms of the quartermaster or the fort's store. That is at the other end of the fort. So it is a second building we do not build, or a mixed-up memory. We build no quartermaster's rooms. A record that cannot pick between two names is not proof of either.
Hubbard names a guard house by the south gate in 1827. That is where a guard house goes, on the gate it watches.

Hubbard names a store house by the south gate in 1827. A book says the rebuilt fort had a food store inside its walls. In 1850 Robert Fergus put a store house on the east side of the open ground. But that was the fort of the 1850s, twenty years after the wall came down. Where the 1830 plan and a man who saw it in 1827 agree, we follow them.
Hubbard names it in 1827. A book says the rebuilt fort had a powder house inside its walls.

Hubbard says the powder house was of brick. It is one of only two brick buildings in the fort. An order from 1803 said powder houses should be brick and shaped like a cone. But that was for the first fort. It does not prove this one was a cone. It is built as a plain block with a roof of two slopes.

Made up, on a side we know. Fergus puts the gun house on the east side of the parade ground, with the barracks and the store house. The 1830 plan draws just one building on that side, and we read it as the barracks. So there is no drawn building for this one. We put it at the south end of the east wall, the one empty spot. Every number is ours.

Made up. It is 40 by 25 feet, borrowed from a hotel nearby. No record gives a size. South Water lots were 55 feet wide, and 40 fits inside that. A bigger doubt than the size: nothing says the paper had its own building. It may have rented rooms in someone else's. Andreas says so when he means rooms, as for the other paper. For this one he only says where the office was. Building a whole house here is our biggest guess in this record.

Our guess. 40 by 25 feet, a size borrowed from the Green Tree inn. Nothing is known about this building. We use the bigger size because a book says it was a food store and also a shipping shop. That is two trades under one roof, and they need room for barrels. That is a reason from the trade, not the building. A lot on South Water was 55 feet wide, and 40 feet fits inside.

Our guess. 40 by 25 feet, a size borrowed from the Green Tree inn. Nothing is known about this building. We use the bigger size because a shipping house keeps other men's goods, and needs room for them. That is a reason from the trade, not the building. A lot on South Water was 55 feet wide, and 40 feet fits inside.

Our guess. 40 by 25 feet, a size borrowed from the Green Tree inn. Nothing is known about this building's size. The 55 foot lot width is for South Water Street, not Lake Street, so no limit is claimed here. We use 40 feet because it is the one size we can borrow, not because anything says it was that wide.

Made up. It is 40 by 25 feet, borrowed from a hotel nearby. No record gives a size. A warehouse was likely bigger than this, and we do not claim otherwise. Storing barrels and hides needs room, and this is a big room, not a warehouse. We use this size because it is the one borrowed size we can stand behind. A bigger made-up size would be more made up, not less.

Our guess, and on purpose the biggest box on this land. 50 by 30 feet. No record gives its size. But the one thing the record does say is about how much it held. Hubbard packed about five thousand hogs in it in the season of 1834. A man does not do that in a 40 by 25 foot shop. So the box is made bigger for that reason alone. That reason is weaker than it looks, and we should say so. A packing season lasts months. Hogs come in and barrels go out all the time. The building needed to hold a day's work, not a season's. The 55 foot limit on South Water lots does not apply to Lake Street.

Made up, and made as a cabin, not a barn. Andreas gives no size. 20 by 16 feet is a one-room log cabin, the smallest home built here. The book tells of a house that became a barn. Beaubien did not build a barn. He moved out and left the cabin as one. So we keep it cabin-sized. 20 feet comes from Hogan's store, and 16 feet is a common depth. Every number is made up.

Our guess, and the math behind it is given so it can be argued with. No record gives its size. What is known is its cost, about $900, and that it had two floors. We also know the cost and size of two other buildings of the time. The Presbyterian church cost $600 for 1,000 square feet. St Mary's cost $400 for 875 square feet. In between, about 55 cents a square foot, $900 buys about 1,600 square feet, or 800 a floor. 30 by 25 feet is 750 square feet, a little under. That is close, and on the safe side. It is still a guess, marked as one. A second floor costs less than a roof and base, so the real building may have been bigger. The 25 foot depth is borrowed too, from both churches.

Made up, and a record could easily have told us. Nothing says what the house was built of. We chose sawn wood. The work here was done by hired carpenters under Samuel Jackson, for the government. A house next to a stone tower in 1832 could just as well be wood or logs. That is a guess about the time and who paid, not about this house. Logs would be just as fair a guess.

Made up, but kept small, as the record says. Andreas calls it a small store and gives no size. So it is the second smallest building here, 25 by 20 feet. Both numbers are borrowed. 20 feet comes from Hogan's store, the one log building here whose size is known. 25 feet comes from the rooms of a hotel nearby. Lots on South Water were 55 feet wide. This store uses less than half of that, which is what small should look like.

Our guess, taken from the other crossing, since both cross the same kind of water. Our notes put the bottom of these wet ditches 1.5 to 3 feet below the land around them. So a deck at street level sits about half a meter over the water. Under this deck the water is only 0.17 to 0.38 meters deep. Nothing passed under it. The six feet under the big river bridges was for a winter road, and does not fit a ditch.

Made up. It is 40 by 25 feet, the same size we use for every store on South Water whose size no one wrote down. That comes from a hotel nearby. Neither Andreas nor the paper gives a size. Lots here were 55 feet wide, so 40 fits. It is built as a whole building, not just an office. Andreas says Calhoun got an office in a building, so the press was in part of a bigger house. The same first paper has an ad for the new store on that same corner. A building with a store and a print shop is not a shed.

Our guess, but inside a known plan. Andreas says two rooms and says logs. So it is two log rooms side by side. 30 by 18 feet is two rooms of about 15 by 18 feet. It is smaller than the one like it that we know. Hogan's log store is 45 by 20 feet, and held a store and a post office. Andreas uses that size to show how little room the town needed. A house he calls only a log house of two rooms should not be as big. So the front is cut by a third and the depth by two feet. That is a reason about its kind, not this building. A lot on South Water was 55 feet wide, and this fits well inside.

Every number is our guess. 8 by 14 feet fits our sizes for a small work shed. Hides are hung to dry out of the sun and rain. That wants a long, narrow shed with air through it, not a room. Nothing says this yard had a drying shed.

Made up. It is 8 by 14 feet, a small shed. Soap is boiled with lye, and lye comes from soaking wood ash. Ash must stay dry under a roof, or it is no good. So this is the shed that keeps the ash dry. Nothing says this soap works had one. Every number is made up.

Our guess. 8 by 16 feet fits our sizes for a wood shed or store shed, which is what a salt house is. The size is from our list. Nothing says this plant had a salt house, or how big. What we can say is that salt came up the lake in barrels and was used by the barrel. So this is a small store between the landing and the packing floor, not a big store house. Every number is our guess, and no record is given.

Every number is our guess. 8 by 16 feet fits our sizes for a wood shed or a store shed. A bark shed was a store. Bark from trees was brought in, kept dry, and ground up when it was needed. The size is from our list. Nothing says this yard had a bark shed at all.

Every number is our guess. 18 by 26 feet is the smallest of our sizes for a stable with a loft. Smallest, because this is a shed for animals waiting to be killed, and for the plant's own work oxen, not a stable for hire. 300 cattle in a whole season is a few animals at a time, not a herd.

Made up. No record gives a size, a plan or how many rooms. It is about 46 by 30 feet. That is between two hotels nearby, one 40 by 25 feet and one with a 40-foot front. This was Beaubien's second, later house, built while the town was booming. It held a hotel and a public room. None of that is proof about this building. Old papers could settle it. The house was an address in both of the town's papers, and a hotel ad of the time would count its rooms.

Made up. No record tells of a window. Five windows across 40 feet puts one every 8 feet, a usual spacing then. Our builder would give four, but a door in the middle needs an odd number. So five comes from how we build, not from a finding. A picture or a description could settle it.

Our guess. No record tells of a door or window on this building. Three across, a door in the middle with a window on each side, and the same above, is the plainest even front we build. Our builder would pick three for a 30 foot front anyway, so the number is not made bigger. It is still a guess about a front no one told of.
Made up. No record gives a size. It is about 26 by 16 feet, a shed big enough for three small cannon and their carts. We sized it to fit the empty spot, not from proof.

Made up. No record gives a size. It is 40 by 25 feet, borrowed from two hotels in town. An auction room is one big room full of standing people, with no walls inside. So a plain box is at least the right kind of shape. That comes from what the room was for, not from a record of it.

Our guess. No record gives its size, and the plan does not draw it. 15 by 12 feet is a powder house for a fort this size, and no more. We build it because two records tell of a brick building. But what you see of its shape is our math.

Our guess. No record says where Harmon's cabin was. What we know is where it was not. His land of 140 acres went up to about Sixteenth Street. That is two kilometers south of the town we build, and a farm, not a home. This cabin sits on the south side, where we put older log homes. It is a guess inside the right part of town.

Made up. No record gives the tower's width or shape. At first we made it 5.6 meters wide, what a 40-foot stone tower of the time would need. Now it is about 3 meters across, to fit an old print of the harbor. The middle stays in the same spot. The print helps with how it looks, but it gives no true size. This is our best try so far, not a match.

Made up. Nothing tells of a door. People walked in and out of a trading post with goods in their arms. So it gets a door for one person. A wider door would claim wagons came here, and nothing says so.

Our guess. Nothing is known about this building. 25 by 20 feet is our small shop size here. 20 feet is the known depth of Hogan's store. 25 feet comes from the Green Tree's rooms. A drug store is the smallest kind of shop on the street. That is the only reason we use the small size, not the 40 by 25. A lot on South Water was 55 feet wide, and this fits well inside.

Our guess. Nothing at all is known about this building. 30 by 20 feet is the smallest shop on this lot's South Water front. The one thing the record hints at is that it was one of several shops along a street, not a corner building. The 20 foot depth is Hogan's store's, the one size from that time we have. The 30 foot front fits well inside a 55 foot lot. Both sizes are borrowed. Neither is proof about this building.
Made up. The door is on the north side, the same way the house faces. So the post's door and the house's door face the same way.
The house was painted white, so it had boards on the outside. Long boards that lap over each other were the usual then. Not known for sure.

It was an inn all through these years. The bar room was the office and front desk. The dining room was cleared for dancing. There were rooms above, and beds in the attic when it was full. By 1844 it was called the Chicago Hotel. That is after 1835, and only a new sign, not a new trade.

Ingersoll ran it from 1834 to 1837, which covers 1 July 1835, with Martin Ford. A book lists David Clark and then Edward Parsons, with no dates. That fits too. Clark is named as the man who opened the inn in 1833, before Ingersoll.
How tall the door is, used to size the window. The picture has no scale. So the door is about as tall as a person, our usual, not a measure.
