Its builder, W. H. Stow, says it was built in 1834. The list of hotels says it opened in 1835.

John Gray said there should be a small attic window in the pointed end, for we used the attic too. A pointed end with a window in it tells us what kind of roof it had. That is rare in our records. The front is on Canal and the long side on Lake. So the pointed ends face east and west, and the top of the roof runs along Lake Street.

Juliette Kinzie lived inside it in 1831. She wrote that the fort was fenced in by high posts, with strong corners at every other corner. A book calls it a square fence of posts. A line of tall posts set in the ground is what both tell of. It is the one thing about this wall that two records say.

Kinzie wrote in 1831 about the soldiers' root houses on the bank west of the fort. So whose they were is in her words. This is the second one she tells of. Where it stood is not said. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 it was the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

Kinzie wrote in 1831 about the soldiers' root houses on the bank west of the fort. So whose they were is in her words. Where on the bank they stood is not. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 these were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

Logs are still our guess from how people built here. They are not known for this house. Beaubien's 1817 buy was a different house, the Dean house. 1822 is the earliest it could be, not a known year it was built. Wentworth wrote a note under his 1831 picture of the town. It puts Beaubien's house near the same corner as this one. So this is our best guess for which house it is. Both clues come from Wentworth, not from two different people. Where the house came from and how it looked in July 1835 are still not known. Nothing from a picture or from the trading house is used here.

March 1832. Our record used to say 1833 and cite a book for it, but the book never gives 1833. It gives 1832 both times it tells of the pen. It says that in March 1832, Samuel Miller built the so-called stray pen on the corner of the square. People called it the first public building in Chicago. It was a small wooden fence with no roof. The book's list of dates puts it under 1832 too. We read the month right but the year from the wrong line. Nothing in the scene changes. The pen stands in July 1835, with no roof, either way. We fix it because citing a book for something it does not say is the kind of mistake this project cares about most. The end date is just where our record stops. The pen stopped holding prisoners in the fall of 1833, when the log jail went up nearby.

Measured, and bigger than a blockhouse should be. It is about 48 by 32 feet, read from the 1830 plan. A blockhouse then was usually 20 to 30 feet square. So either this one was big, or, more likely, the plan drew the blockhouse and the wall around it as one heavy block. We keep the measure, not shrink it to the usual size. Shrinking it would put a rule of thumb ahead of the only plan we have. It could be off by a quarter.

No record dates either end. Both are the honest limits of what is known. The start is McKee's own arrival. A book says he was hired as the blacksmith the 1821 treaty called for. He reached Fort Dearborn in June 1823, and found only two houses on the north side of the river. He built the fourth himself. 1823 is the first year he could have kept a house here. The end is the weakest line in this record. A book tells of the place about 1830, and Wau-Bun in 1831. After that, nothing names this building. The case for 1835 is that the Potawatomi were still owed a blacksmith by the treaties of 1821 and 1833. That is about a promise, not a house. So it is marked as our guess.

No record dates either end. The start is the light itself. Samuel Jackson finished the second tower in 1832. Samuel Lasby was the first keeper, paid $350 a year, with a place to live. A keeper's house is not newer than its light. The end is just where our record stops, not when the house came down. Both ends are our guess.

Our guess. No size is known. 20 by 26 feet is at the small end of our sizes for a stable. That is room for a doctor's horse, a light cart and the hay above them. A doctor who rode out to the sick kept that much.

No record dates this building at either end. Andreas says David McKee was the government's blacksmith, with a shop near the Agency House. McKee came here in June 1823, so that is the first year the shop could stand. Records show the shop around 1830 and 1831. After that, nothing. McKee had other work by then. He carried the mail from 1827, and later farmed. But by treaties of 1821 and 1833, the Potawatomi were still owed a government blacksmith in 1835. That is why we think the shop still stood. It is a guess about a promise, not about a building.
No record tells of the tents. We have two kinds. The pointed one is small and cheap. A family on the road with a wagon would carry that one.
No record tells of the tents. We use two kinds, one after the other, both sold by shops in the 1830s.
No record tells of the tents. Two kinds, square ones and pointed ones, were what shops and the army sold in the 1830s. A family landing at Chicago carried what it had bought in the East, or sewn.

No record gives a size. It is about 47 by 31 feet, measured from the drawing on the plan. It could be off by a fifth. The long side is the front. What backs the size is the plan's own word. It is the only building on the sheet the drawer called big. A 47-foot barn is big for this town in 1830, but not odd for a fort with horses, hay and a four-acre field.

No record gives a size. It is about 67 by 26 feet, measured from the drawing on the plan. It could be off by a fifth. The block is drawn as a heavy bar, and the ink inside it has faded. So this is the outside of the bar, the most it could be, not a close guess. The size helps name it. 67 by 26 feet is a trading house with a store and a home in it. It is the only one of the three blocks big enough for the two floors Hubbard tells of.

No record gives a size. It is about 3.9 by 2.9 meters, measured from the drawing on the plan. It could be off by a fifth. The block is filled in, not drawn as a line. So this is the outside of the ink, the most it could be, not a close guess.

No record gives a size. It is about 7.3 by 5.8 meters, measured from the drawing on the plan. It could be off by a fifth. The block is filled in, not drawn as a line. So this is the outside of the ink, the most it could be, not a close guess.

No record gives a size. It is about 31 by 15 feet, measured from the drawing on the plan. It could be off by a fifth. The long side is the front. It lines up with the fort, not with north. Whoever built it set it square to the fort.
No record gives a size. It is about 32 by 24 feet, measured from the drawing on the plan. It could be off by a fifth. It is the most square of the three buildings here, as the plan draws it.

No record gives its size. It is about 36 by 14 feet, the west one of two small buildings by the south wall, as drawn on the 1830 plan. Trust the 14-foot depth least. On the plan it is only a few dots wide, and the drawn line takes up much of that.

No record gives its size. It is about 40 by 14 feet, the east one of two small buildings by the south wall, as drawn on the 1830 plan. The same warning as the one next to it: the depth is a very small measure on the map.

No record gives its size. It is about 49 by 21 feet, the north-east building as drawn on the 1830 plan. It comes out nearly the same length as the leader's house across from it. That is what the plan draws, not a guess. It could be off by a fifth.

No record gives its size. It is about 90 by 36 feet, as drawn on the 1830 plan. We measured the plan's scale from another building. It is the biggest building in the fort, as a barracks for two groups of soldiers should be. That is our only check. It could be off by a fifth, and the depth more than the length.

No one told of the middle of this bridge, and none is the answer that makes up least. Our builder allows it: a short crossing goes end to end with nothing in the water. Without a number, it would put a support in the middle of an 8 meter span. An 8 meter log needs no support in the middle. The river bridges needed two each over 56 and 72 meters. So the number comes from the span, and keeps a post out of a stream no one says had one.

This is not how many chimneys the finished hotel had. No one records that. A building one floor up has no chimneys standing above it yet. It also has no roof top to put them on. A guess from how far it was built, not from a record.

Not an inn on the day we show. That is the most important fact here. Miller's inn competed with the Wolf Point inn from 1830. But Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, already calls the Miller house empty at this time. Miller had moved to what was becoming Michigan City. A book says it became a store, run by Peck, after 1832. Another says Miller left the trade in 1834. The three do not agree on dates, but all point the same way. So we show it standing, used as a store or home, not an inn. Peck running it does not last to 1835 either. Our own notes put Peck in 1835 at his store of two floors at South Water and LaSalle.

Most likely it was not used as the agency's office in 1835. We have little proof. A book says it was left empty when Dr. Wolcott died in 1830. In the fall of 1832, the book calls it the old agency house where Colonel Hamilton then lived. Hamilton worked for the county. He lived in it as a home while the agency's work came to an end after the 1833 treaty. Nothing says who was in it in July 1835, or what it was used for. So we call it a home and place no one here.

Not known either way, but our builder needs a choice, so leaving it out would pick one without saying. Bare gray boards are our usual for a new part on an inn in a frontier town. A book backs it a little. At Wolf Point in 1831, one white painted building was the wonder of the town, because the buildings around it were not painted. Still, it is a choice.

Not known either way. We must choose a color, or it would be painted white by default, and that would be a claim too. One thing makes us wonder. The man who built it also built the Sauganash, a white house with bright blue shutters that people admired. So he might have painted this one. Nothing says he did. Bare wood is the cheaper choice for a house built fast in a boom. It is still a choice.

Not known either way. But our builder needs a choice, and leaving it out would paint the building white. That would be a claim. Wau-Bun's story of the Sauganash's white paint, the wonder of Wolf Point in 1831, shows it was worth pointing out then. Bare boards are the cheaper reading for a house built fast in the boom of 1835, and still a choice.

No record says, so this is a guess from how it was used. The paper had an office here, and a store sold goods from the same corner. So at least two businesses shared it. A building with two floors was the usual way to do that on a corner. Peck's store, a block away, had two floors. It might have had one floor, and then it would be shorter. A drawing in the paper shows a three-floor building, but that was a stock picture, not this house. We do not use it.

Not known for this crossing, and on purpose not the river bridges' known size. Charles Cleaver said those bridges were ten feet wide. That is proof about the two river bridges, and we use it there. Here it is only a guide. 3 meters is a little under it. Our guess is that a bridge carrying a public street was about a wagon wide. No one built a street crossing wider than the town's main river bridges. Read the number as about a wagon's width, not a measure.

Not known. This number stands for a little way back from the street. The book says the log inn stood back and the frame part reached the street. It does not say how far back. So the depth of the new part is the size of a gap no one measured. 4 meters is about 13 feet. That leaves 5 meters of log building behind it, enough to still be a building. Anything from a porch two meters deep to a whole second building fits the sentence.

Not known, and not worked out either. The plan draws a filled box with a label. It says nothing about what it was made of, and no other record tells of these buildings. Logs are our usual choice for a small building at a fort whose main buildings were logs. It is marked as our guess.

Not known. The other choice was logs. Bonnell says nothing about what it was made of. In 1835 Chicago had built with light wood frames for three years. The first was St Mary's church in 1833. The east end of the north bank was new land, built on by men with money. So a light frame house is our choice. It is marked as our guess, since there is nothing about this building to work from.

Not known. 5.2 meters is about 17 feet, two floors of the time, plus floors between and a base. We use the same height for other buildings with two floors. It depends on the number of floors, which is a guess.

Not known. 5.2 meters is about 17 feet, two floors of the usual height with the floors between. It is the same as the Miller house's part with two floors. It is as unsure as the number of floors, which is a guess too.

Not known. The book gives the new part what it was made of, a side and a year, but no height. One floor is chosen because the log inn it was added to has one floor with a loft. A front of two floors on a log inn of one floor would be more special, and would likely have been said. That reason is from silence, so it is marked as a weaker guess.
Not known. A roof with two slopes was the usual roof for a wood building of this kind and time. Nothing says so of this one.
Not known. One floor is usual for a village shop opened in 1833. We give it to the other shops in the same paper too. It is our choice.

Not known. The door is on the side facing the river, with no proof. The water is where the landing was, and where the waste went. If the animals came in over the prairie, the door belongs on the other side. It is marked as our guess, not left to a default.

Not known. The door is on the north side, because our guess at which way it faces puts the inn's back yard there. Nothing says which way it faced, and no reading is better than another. It is marked as our guess, not left to a default.
No record says. The door faces north, toward the house, because that is the yard side where we placed it. If the barn stood the other way, the door goes somewhere else. We mark it as a guess.

Not known. The frame part runs the full 12 meter front, so it covers the whole front of the log part and shows one face to Lake Street. Out to the street line tells how it ended, not how wide it was. A narrower part would leave a notch at one end. No record tells of one, and it would look like a fact about the plan. This size follows our rule, not a finding, and the building's shape is our guess too.

No record says. The door faces the river, the same way the front faces. That is where the landing and the water were. Nothing says the animals came by water, not across the prairie. If they came by land, the door belongs on the other side. We mark it as a guess.
Not known. The front faces north, so the door faces the alley, where a stable's carts and horses went.
Not known. The front faces south, so the door faces the alley where we put a stable's traffic.

Not known. The house was painted, so it had boards on it, so it was a frame, not logs. That much follows from yellow. Which kind of frame is not known. We give the older kind, since this was a small house on sand at the edge of town, kept by a man who pulled stumps. That is our guess about who built it.
Not known. A town hotel in 1834 had two floors, but no record says so of this one. We chose it.

No record says, and no record we found tells what any small back building at the forks was made of. Logs are our guess from the date and the bank. The inn it served is itself logs, with a frame part. A website calls the Wolf Point buildings of these years log. Chicago had no sawn wood of its own until the mills of 1832 and 1833, after this building must have stood. The same reason that gives boards for the Western Hotel's stable of 1834 gives logs here. We grade both the same way, for opposite answers, on purpose. If the stable was rebuilt or boarded after the mills opened, this is the earlier of two states, and the record does not know it.

No record says. No record we found tells what any small back building at the forks was made of. Boards nailed up and down, with gaps, is our guess from the date and from the hotel it belonged to. The hotel is a frame house of two floors from 1834. By then Chicago had a steam saw mill, and wood was coming in by ship. A man who framed a 40 by 60 foot hotel would board his stable from the same pile. Logs fit the west bank of 1828 to 1831, not a new house of 1834. If the stable was an older log building that Stow built next to, this record has the right shape with the wrong walls.

No record says. It is built of sawn boards, like another hotel's stable from 1834. By the time this hotel took guests, the town's sawmills were cutting boards. A stable is what a hotel keeper built quickest and cheapest. An older stable nearby was logs, but that was an earlier time.

Neither record says, and two guesses pull opposite ways. We take the one that claims less. For logs: every fort building here is logs. The soldiers built with trees they cut. A barn is the last to get sawn wood. Against logs: a cupola is fine work, and fits a sawn wood barn better. We chose logs. It is the usual guess here.

Nothing at all is known about how tall it was. Warehouses then ran from one-floor sheds to stores with two and a half floors. The choice changes its shape by half. We give it one floor, because that claims less. It is made up, and marked so.

Nothing in any record says where these works stood. The ad and the book name the business, but no street. So this spot is our idea, and no record backs it. We had two reasons. First, Elston is tied to the North Branch. A road there is named for him, and his later brickyard was on that side. But that is not 1833. Second, making soap and candles means boiling fat, and it smells very bad. Smelly work sat at the edge of town, on water, near the butchers who sold the fat. But towns do not always follow that rule. Another guess is just as good: the ads all came from near South Water Street, and he wanted ashes from people's homes. So treat this spot as an idea. One line of an ad from 1834 or 1835 could fix it.

Nothing is known. A hand press, boxes of letters and a worker fit in one room. A three-week-old paper could be in a shop with one floor or two. We give it one, because that claims less. It is made up, and marked so.

Named as the man who built it. That is what the record says, and all it says: built by Thomas Church. If he kept the store himself, or if anyone was in it on 1 July 1835, is not said. It is marked as our guess for that reason.

Named as the man who built it and ran it. He came from Vermont on 8 October 1833. A book tells of his later life in Chicago. He was a city leader in 1843 and 1844, with two streets named after him. That backs the man, but says nothing about who was at the anvil in July 1835.
Three records name it as the officers' rooms. Hubbard did in 1827. A book on the new fort did. So did the list of 1855.
Hubbard named it in 1827, and a book about the rebuilt fort did too. Both put it on the east side.
Our usual window panes, until we know more. The exact panes are not known from either picture.
Our usual plan only. The rooms inside are not known. The picture sets the windows and door on the front.

No proof either way, and we have no picture of this building. No porch is our usual, not a finding. It is a real open question. A wagon house with gates to its yard from both streets is just the kind of building that often had a porch over the front door. Nothing here rules one out.

No record gives a height for this house. 2.75 meters is our usual for one floor. It comes from the one ceiling height we know, the Green Tree's seven and a half feet, plus the floor. It is as unsure as the number of floors.

No record gives a size. 0.25 meters is a lighter log than the 0.30 meters of the river bridges. A log is sized to how far it reaches, and this one reaches a seventh as far. A guess about carpentry, not a measure.

No record gives a size. 0.25 meters is the same as the Slough Log Bridge, for the same reason. A log is sized to how far it reaches. These two reach 8 and 12 meters. The river bridges reach 56 and 72, with logs of 0.30 meters.

No record gives a size. 0.26 meters is between the other crossing's 0.25 and the river bridges' 0.30. The reason is the same: a log is sized to how far it reaches. With one support, this one reaches 6 meters. The other reaches 8, and the river bridges 18 to 24. It comes from how carpenters built, not a measure.
No record gives a number. 2.3 meters is about 8 feet, the wall of a one-room log house. We use the same height for another log cabin and for the blacksmith shop next door.

No record gives a number. 2.4 meters is about 8 feet at the roof edge. That is enough to stand and push a cart under, and to pile the new bricks a few rows high. We set it ourselves. Our usual height for a shed this long would be 3 meters, and that would make a low work shed look like a house.
No record gives a number. 2.4 meters is about 8 feet, the wall of a one-room log house. We use the same height for another log cabin and for the blacksmith shop next door.

No record gives a number. 2.4 meters is about 8 feet, the wall of a one-room log house. A real blacksmith shop might have been taller, for the heat and smoke. No one wrote that, but if a record ever does, this number would go up.
No record gives a number. 2.4 meters is about 8 feet, the same as the other small homes here.

No record gives a height. 2.5 meters is about 8 feet, one floor of wall. We use it for our other log buildings with one floor. The church a block away had posts twelve feet tall. That is a different, taller building. So this number is our guess, not borrowed.

No record gives a number. 2.5 meters is about 8 feet, one floor of log wall. We use the same height for Hogan's store and other log buildings. A stable door 2.3 meters tall in this wall leaves just a little wood above it. That is not a mistake. The wall was built for a person, and the door was cut for a horse. So we set the wall's height ourselves, and do not let the door get more room than the cabin had.
No record gives a height. 2.5 meters is about 8 feet, one floor of squared logs. It is the same as Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

No record gives a height. 2.5 meters is about 8 feet, one floor of squared logs. It is the same as Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house, our other log buildings with one floor. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 2.5 meters.

No record gives a height. 2.5 meters is about 8 feet, one floor of squared logs. It is the same as the Walker meeting house, our other log building with one floor. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 2.5 meters.
No record gives a height. 2.5 meters is about 8 feet, one floor of squared logs. It is the same as Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.
No record gives a number. 2.6 meters is about 8 and a half feet, a log wall of one floor, as we build others on this bank. A room for meetings might have been taller. Nothing says so.

No record gives a number. 2.8 meters is about 9 feet at the roof edge. That gives room over a kettle on a fire, with air above. It is more than a store needs and less than a warehouse. We set it ourselves, not our usual 3.18 meters. Our guess is the range and the reason, not the exact number.

No record gives a number. 2.8 meters is about 9 feet, a log wall a little taller than a home's. A butcher's floor needs that, to hang an animal up. We set it ourselves. Our usual height for a building this size would be 3.55 meters, and it would look like it had two floors. Our guess is only that the wall was about this tall.

The range is our reason, not the number. No record gives a height. 2.8 meters is about 9 feet, a log wall of about nine rows. It is a row or two taller than a house, because a horse is led in under a beam, and something is stored above it. It is just under our usual for this size.

No record gives a height. 3 meters is about 10 feet to the roof edge. That is room to swing a big hammer and stand a horse inside, with air over the fire. It is close to our usual for this size. We give our own number so the reason for it is on the record.
No record gives a height. 3 meters is about 10 feet, one floor of shop with room over a counter. Our guess is that the wall was about this tall, not exactly 3 meters.
No record gives a number. 3 meters is about 10 feet, one floor of a store, a little taller than a home. We are not sure how many floors it had, so we are not sure of this either.
No record gives a height. 3 meters is about 10 feet, one floor of shop. It is as unsure as the number of floors.
No record gives a height. 3 meters is about 10 feet, one floor of shop. It is as unsure as the number of floors.

No record gives a height. 3.2 meters is about 10 and a half feet to the roof. It is a little lower than the Presbyterian church, because this building is smaller, cost a third less for its size, and was called rough. The one ceiling height we know is the Green Tree's seven and a half feet. A room of 875 square feet holding a church crowd needed more than that. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 3.2 meters.

No record gives a height. 3.2 meters is about 10 and a half feet, room to work on a killing floor, where animals were hung up. It is taller than a house wall, and lower than our usual for this size, which would look like a building with a room above. The range is our reason, not the number.

No record gives a number. 3.2 meters is about 10 and a half feet, one floor of a shop. It is a little taller than a home, since a press is worked standing up. We are not sure how many floors it had, so we are not sure of this either.

Our guess. No record gives a height. 3.2 meters is near the bottom of our sizes for a house of a floor and a half. It is lower than Dr. Kimberly's house next door, because one record calls this house small. It is the lowest wall we can build here. Any lower, and no one could stand up in the room below. So the height comes from our rule for room to stand, not a record.

No record gives a height. 3.4 meters is about 11 feet to the roof edge. It is a tall floor with storage in the roof, how a shipping house worked: goods in at ground level off the dock, kept above. A taller wall would look like two full floors, and that would be a claim. A book tells of the firm's later store house lifting wheat to the upper floor with men and a rope. But that is the 1839 building. It shows how it was done, not this building.

The range is our reason, not the number. No record gives a height. 3.4 meters is about 11 feet. The number comes from what goes on inside. A horse is led in and out under a beam, and hay is thrown over the stalls. A wall much under 3 meters makes a stable a shed. A longer row of stalls does not change that, so we keep 3.4 meters.

No record gives a height. 3.4 meters is the low end of our sizes for a house of a floor and a half. It is one floor of the one ceiling height we know in Chicago, the Green Tree's seven and a half feet, plus the floor and the low wall under the roof. Our guess for this building, and low, since nothing here is known.

No record gives a height. 3.6 meters is about 12 feet to the roof, for a house of a floor and a half. That is a full floor, built up from the Green Tree's known seven and a half foot ceiling, with a low wall above. It is our usual for this number of floors. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 3.6 meters.
No record gives a height. 3.6 meters is about 12 feet, one floor, built taller than a house, for piled up goods and a cart door. It is as unsure as the number of floors.
No record gives a number. 3.6 meters is about 12 feet, taller than a home. A room full of people bidding, with goods piled up, needs that. This comes from what the room was for, not from a measure.

No record gives a number. 3.6 meters is about 12 feet, one floor, taller than a home. Piled goods and a door for carts need that. We are not sure how many floors it had, so this number is only as good as that guess.
No record gives a height. 3.6 meters is about 12 feet, one floor, built taller than a house, for piled up goods and a cart door. It is as unsure as the number of floors.
No record gives a height. 4 meters is about 13 feet, one floor taller than a shop, as hanging and cutting meat needs. It is as unsure as the number of floors, so it is only as good as that guess.

No record gives a height. 4.9 meters is about 16 feet, two floors built up from the Green Tree's known seven and a half foot ceiling, with the floors between. It is almost the same as our other wood buildings with two floors. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 4.9 meters.
No record gives a height. 5.5 meters is about 18 feet, two floors of 8 feet with the floors between. We use that for our other wood buildings with two floors. It is as unsure as the number of floors.
No record gives a height. 5.5 meters is about 18 feet, two floors of 8 feet with the floors between. We use that for our other wood buildings with two floors, the Sauganash and Peck's store.

No record gives a number. 5.5 meters is about 18 feet, two floors of 8 feet each, with floors between. We use the same height for our other wood buildings with two floors. If it had one floor, this is almost twice too tall. So trust the confidence view more than the shape.

No record gives a height. 5.5 meters is about 18 feet, two floors of 8 feet with the floors between. It is the same as the Sauganash, our other wood building with two floors. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 5.5 meters. It leaves out the loft, which would add a low wall of unknown height.

No record gives a height. 5.5 meters is about 18 feet, two floors of 8 feet with the floors between. It is the same as the Western Hotel, our other wood hotel with two floors. Our guess is that it was about this tall, not exactly 5.5 meters.
No record gives a height. About seven and a half feet, our usual for a building this size. That is room for people to work standing up, and no more. Our guess.

No record gives a height. About 13 feet to the roof edge: a barn that lets a loaded hay wagon through its door, with a loft above. Our usual height for a barn this size is 3.5 meters, so this is only half a meter more.
No record gives a height. It is our usual height for a building this size. Our guess.

No record gives a height for any building at this fort. 5.4 meters is two floors, each about nine feet inside, plus the floors between. That was usual for officers' houses. Our guess is that the wall was about this tall, not exactly 5.4 meters.

No record gives the slope for any building at this fort. 34 degrees is the slope every other fort building here has. It comes from our middle slope for a shingle roof of the time. It is a guess from how roofs were built, not a measure.
No record gives the slope for any building at this fort. 34 degrees is the slope every other fort building here has. Our guess.
No record gives the slope for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is our middle slope for a shingle roof of the time. It is a guess from how roofs were built, not a measure.
No record gives the slope for any building at this fort. 34 degrees is our middle slope for a shingle roof of the time. It is a guess from how roofs were built, not a measure.

No record gives the slope. 18 degrees is our usual slope for a one-sided shed roof. It is about the flattest a roof of split shingles can be and still shed rain. It is a guess from the roof, not a measure.
No record gives the slope. 33 degrees is our middle slope for a small wood shop. It is a guess from how roofs were built, not a measure. We use the same for the other shops in the paper.
No record gives the slope. 35 degrees is our middle slope for a low log building with a roof of split shingles. It is a guess from how people built, not a measure.
