It is a guess from how buildings were made, not a measure. No record gives the slope. 35 degrees is our slope for a low log building with split wood shingles, the same as every other log building here.

No record gives the slope. 35 degrees is our middle slope for a low log building with a roof of split wood shingles. It is the slope on every other log building here. Our sheds are usually less steep, but this was a home first. It is a guess from how people built, not a measure.
It is a guess from how buildings were made, not a measure. No record gives the slope. 38 degrees is a middle slope for roofs of that time.

No record gives the slope. 38 degrees is our middle slope for wood roofs of the time. It is steep enough to shed snow, and low enough for the wood beams of the day. A guess from how roofs were built, not a measure.
It is a guess from how buildings were made, not a measure. No record gives the slope. 38 degrees is the middle slope we use for roofs of two slopes here.
No record gives the slope. 38 degrees is our middle slope for wood roofs of the time. It is a guess from how roofs were built, not a measure. The kind of roof is a guess too.

No record gives the slope. 38 degrees is our middle slope for wood roofs of the time. It is a guess from how roofs were built, not a measure, the same as our other frame buildings. It is a guess about how this kind of roof was built, on a roof shape that is itself a guess.

It is a guess from how buildings were made, not a measure. No record gives the slope. 40 degrees is a middle slope for a log building with wood shingles. It is steep enough to shed snow, low enough for the short roof beams of a log building, and tall enough to give the known loft room to stand.
It is a guess from how buildings were made, not a measure. No record gives the slope. 40 degrees is a middle slope for a log building with split wood shingles.
No record gives the slope. 40 degrees is our usual for a house, and what a shallow house like this has here. It is a choice for the kind, not proof about this house.

It is a guess from how buildings were made, not a measure. No record gives the slope. 40 degrees is our usual here. It is steeper than the 38 we use elsewhere, because the rooms are in the roof. A low roof would put the peak too low to stand under.

No porch with a roof is claimed. A low rail is drawn along the front, as in the picture, with a gap at the door. A low gate in the yard fence comes from our usual parts. A real landing or step is not known.

Not known either way. No record tells the finish of this or any other back building here. Bare gray boards are our usual for a working stable behind a house for wagon drivers. We read the hotel's own boards as bare for the same reason.
No record tells of paint. A bare board stable behind a painted house is the usual guess. Nothing says either way.

No record tells how it was finished. Bare wood is our usual, and a book backs it. Wau-Bun says the white paint on the Sauganash was the wonder of Wolf Point in 1831. The Miller house was right across the water, and was not pointed out that way.

No record tells how it was finished. Not known either way. Bare gray boards are our usual for a working house for wagon drivers on the west side. By 1834 and 1835, paint was less special in Chicago than in 1831. So this guess is weaker here than for the log buildings at Wolf Point.
No record tells of paint. We build it as bare logs, grayed by the weather. That fits an old cabin used on a farm, and it is how we build every other log building here. Nothing says either way.

No record tells how it was finished. Bare gray logs are the usual for this kind. A meeting house that was also a school is the last building at Wolf Point that would be painted, when the inns were not.

No record tells how it was finished. Bare gray logs are our usual. A book backs it. Wau-Bun says one white painted building at Wolf Point in 1831 was the wonder of the town, because the buildings around it were not painted. This inn was one of those buildings.
No record tells how it was finished. Not known either way. Bare gray logs are what we use for every building at Wolf Point in these years, and the inn this one stood behind.

No record tells of a door or window. It gets a stable door, wide enough to lead a horse through by hand. Shoeing horses was half of what a blacksmith out west did. A wider wagon door is tempting, since Pierce did iron work for wagons and coaches. But that work is done on the iron parts, not the whole wagon. A wagon door would also need a taller wall than we claim.

No record tells of a door. Our stable door is wide enough to lead a horse or a cow through, 1.35 meters. It is the smallest door that fits the work. Cattle walked in, 250 of them in 1833 alone. A door for one person would say the killing was done outside, and nothing says that.

No record tells of a door or window. It gets a door wide enough to lead an animal through by hand. 300 cattle in a season needs one. Anything narrower would say the killing was done in a yard, and nothing says that.

No record tells of a door or window. It gets a wagon door, our widest, 2.9 meters, for a loaded wagon. A shipping house needs it. The whole trade is taking goods off wagons and boats, and putting them back on. A narrower door would say it was a shop.

No record tells of a door or window. A store house that moves goods between a dock and the road needs a door a loaded wagon can pass. So it gets a wagon door, 2.9 meters wide. It is a guess from the trade, not from this building.

No record tells of a door. The business took in fat and ashes, and sent out soap and candles. So the door must let barrels and a hand cart through. We use our middle-sized door, 1.35 meters wide. A door for one person would say the work was done in a small room.
No record tells of its front. Evenly spaced windows were the usual for a hotel of two floors this size. That much is safe. How many windows, and how far apart, is our guess.

Not known either way. No record gives the number of floors. One floor with a loft under the roof was the usual log inn of this time and place. It is what the known loft means. Caton's court sat in the unfinished loft, which is a roof space, not a second floor. It is also the safer reading. The records that tell of height in this town point out the Sauganash's two floors, and Miller's frame house of two floors, as special. They would not, if every inn had two.

No record gives the frame part a height. One floor is our guess, for the same reason as the number of floors above. The records that tell of height at Wolf Point point out the Sauganash's two floors and Miller's frame part of two floors as special. They would not, if the Wolf Point inn's frame part had two floors too. A guess, not a record.
No chimney is known. One is our usual, and the smallest claim for a heated house with two floors. A building this big might have had two. We do not guess more. Our guess.
No one says this barn had a loft. It is usual for a barn: hay goes above the floor the wagon uses. It is a guess, and marked so. What you see of it is the hay door in the end wall.
None. A family coming to the forks to trade came by river or on horseback as often as by road. Nothing here says which. So no wagon is drawn, rather than one made up.

Not something to build. It checks the size. $600 for 1,000 square feet is 60 cents a square foot. St. Mary's was $400 for 875 square feet. The Temple Building was $900 for two floors. We sized the Temple Building from this number, so we keep it here.

Not a thing to build, but a check on size. A book says the whole building cost about $400. For 875 square feet, that is 46 cents a square foot. The Presbyterian church cost 60 cents. The two numbers together are what we use to size the Temple Building, whose shape is our guess.

Not known for sure. But a book says its roof edge faced the street. That means a roof with a peak, which for a wood building of this kind, time and place means two slopes. It is worked out from its kind, with a known clue to which way it faces, not a measure.
Not known for 1835. There were soldiers here then, and a book says two groups of them in 1833. We found no count for mid-1835, so no number is given.

Not known for this building. A shipping store house keeps goods above the floor it loads on. We build only one sign of that outside: a door high in the pointed end, where goods were lifted through. Nothing else: no roof window, no floor line, no second row of windows. The book tells of the firm's 1839 store house lifting wheat to the upper floor. That is how it was done, but four years after the day we show.

Not known for this building. A wood frame fits a shop opened in the village in the fall of 1833. By then the town had sawn wood and carpenters. Silas Cobb was a carpenter, and almost for sure the Cobb of this shop. A book says he built the Green Tree inn at this same corner that year. Which kind of frame it was cannot be seen from outside.
Not known for this building. A roof of two slopes is how nearly every small wood building of this kind, time and place was built.
Not known for this building. A roof of two slopes was the usual for both parts of this kind, time and place.
Not known for this building. A roof of two slopes was the usual for frame buildings of this kind, time and place. An L shape means two roofs that cross. Our builder cannot make that yet.
Not known for this building. A roof of two slopes was how nearly every log building of this kind, time and place was roofed. A loft where people sat needs a peaked roof over it.

Not known. The known finishes are inside: plastered walls and bare floors of split logs. Nothing tells of the outside. So it is bare wood boards, grayed by the weather. White paint was rare enough here in 1831 that people wrote about the white Sauganash. The one 1833 church whose outside is known, St. Mary's, was not painted.

Not known for this crossing. Split logs laid flat side up are what the 1883 old settlers' paper tells of on both river bridges, laid on the long logs for a floor. A smaller, rougher street crossing of the same years would not have had a better deck. A guess from how the town built, not from this bridge.

Not known for this crossing. Bent is the old settlers' own word for what stood in the deeper water under the river bridges: four heavy logs resting on the bottom. It is the only one of our three kinds a town would put in half a meter of ditch water. A box filled with stones, or a post pounded into the ground, is not worth the work here.

Not known for this fort. A list from 1808 says the first fort's barracks had two floors and shingle roofs. And two groups of soldiers and their goods do not fit on one floor of a 90-foot building. Both are reasons, but neither is a record of the 1816 fort.

No record says. A roof with one slope is the cheapest roof. It is the usual roof for a drying shed. A drying shed keeps rain off new bricks while air moves under it. So we build it as a shed roof on purpose.

Not known here. Split logs laid flat side up are what the 1883 old settlers' paper tells of on both river bridges. A smaller, rougher crossing on the town's quietest street would not have had a better deck.
No record says. It is a safe guess. A blacksmith shop is one tall room with a forge, and every building in this group was small and made of logs.

No record says. Compact little building and two large rooms both sound like one floor. A house that grew by adding wings and back parts is a house that could not grow up. The same book tells of the first agency house, from 1803, which had two floors. That is a different building. So this is a guess.
Not known. A 90-foot barracks split into rooms needed a chimney for each group of rooms. Three is the least that would heat a building this long. The count is our guess.
Not known. A building used for church and school through Chicago winters needed heat. One chimney is the least, and the usual, for a log building of one room. A guess, not proof.
No record says. A council house is a hall, one tall room. Every log building nearby is said to have one floor. This is a guess from its kind and its use.
No record says. A home here cooked and kept warm at a fireplace, so it has one chimney. We put it on the end wall. No record says where it really stood.
Not known. A school of one room from 1833 had one floor, as that kind did. Nothing about Watkins's schools says it was any other way.
Not known. A powder house is one room on one floor, as that kind of building always is.
No record says. A house for one keeper at a lonely light had one floor, like the other small homes here.

Not known. A log house of one room was the usual at the forks in 1831. A building put to a trade is the last one anyone would build a second floor on. A guess from its kind, not from a record about this building.
Not known. The fort's store is a shop with a store room. One floor is usual. The 1830 plan draws it as deep as the small south buildings, not the long ones.
Not known. The number is our guess. A hotel of two floors this size needed several fireplaces. Two chimneys is the usual least for an L of this shape.
Not known. Long boards over a wood frame were the usual finish for this kind of building, time and place.
No record says. Every writer calls these houses small and made of logs, and nothing more. So it is a one-room log house, one floor high, like the blacksmith shop next door.
Not known. A roof of two slopes is our usual. The only other kind we build slopes one way, and a house with two floors does not have that. Our guess.
Not known. Almost every wood building of this kind had a roof with two slopes. Our only other choice, a one-sided roof, would not work over a building this deep.
Not known. A roof of two slopes was the usual roof for a wood house of this kind, time and place. The rooms under the roof need its pointed ends.
Not known. A roof of two slopes was the usual roof for a wood house of this kind, time and place. The rooms under it get light from its pointed ends.

Not known. Worked out from its kind. A roof of two slopes was the usual for a wood house of this time and place. We build no other kind over a floor and a half. The half floor is the roof, and its rooms get light from the pointed ends.
Not known. A roof with two slopes was the usual roof for a long building then. It is also how the building looks in the 1855 photo. A guess from its kind.
Not known. A roof of two slopes was the usual roof for a small wood house of this time and place. A roof that slopes one way is not what a house for sale this size would have.
Not known. Worked out from its kind. A roof of two slopes was the usual for a wood building of two floors at this time and place. We do not put a roof that slopes one way over a building this deep.

Not known. A roof of two slopes was the usual roof for a wood building of this kind, time and place. A building with a loft people use under the roof has two slopes, as that kind did. Worked out from its kind, not a measure.
No record says. Almost every wood building of this kind had a roof with two slopes. It is also the simplest roof for one big room.
No record says. Almost every wood building of this kind, in this time and place, had a roof with two slopes.
No record says. Almost every wood building of this kind, in this time and place, had a roof with two slopes. That is a guess from the kind of building, not a measure.

Not known. A roof of two slopes was how nearly every log building of this kind, time and place was roofed. A log building 6 meters deep is too deep for a roof that slopes one way. Our builder would pick two slopes for this depth anyway. We say so, so the choice comes with its reason.
Not known. A roof of two slopes was how nearly every log building of this kind, time and place was roofed. A 45 foot building this deep got one, unless something says not.
Not known. A roof of two slopes was how nearly every log building of this kind, time and place was roofed. Two log rooms like these got one, unless something says not.
No record says. Almost every log house of this kind, in this time and place, had a roof with two slopes.

Not known. A roof of two slopes was how nearly every log building of this kind, time and place was roofed. A roof leaning on the Sauganash's east wall is the one other choice. Right next to could mean that. We note it here but do not build it, since no record tells how the two buildings met.
No record says. Almost every log house of this kind, in this time and place, had a roof with two slopes. That is a guess from the kind of building, not a measure.

No record says. It gets a roof with two slopes, not the one slope a shed would have. That is because it was a cabin before it was a barn. A cabin here had a two-sided roof over a loft. A one-sided roof would make it look built as a shed, and the book says it was not.

No record says. New bricks have to dry in moving air, out of the rain. So a drying shed is a roof on posts, open along its long side, not a closed building. One open side is the safe guess. Two would make it a shed you could drive through. This is a guess about how the work was done, not about this shed.
Not known. The number is our guess. One chimney is the least an inn with a public room and cooking needed. A log building this size would rarely have more.
Not known. One chimney is the least a shop needs to stay open through a Chicago winter. The number is the guess. Everything else about the chimney is our usual.
No record says. A man who watched a light all night, through a Chicago winter, cooked and kept warm at a fireplace. So the house has one chimney. No record says where. We put it on the end wall.
Not known. Evenly spaced windows are the usual for this kind, and what our builder draws. No record tells of a window on this building.

Not known. The door is on the north side, facing the yard and the back of the hotel. That is the side the record fills with life. The yard is where the teams stood, and where the gates from both streets led. A stable door on any other side would open onto the lots next door. A guess from the yard, not a record about the building.
Not known. The smallest of our three door kinds, which is the smallest claim. Our guess.

Not known. Our guess. A floor and a half, with rooms under the roof, was the usual kind of house then. It is the only way a house called small could hold all the boarders it was full of. They slept in the rooms under the roof.
Not known. A floor and a half was the usual house of these years, and our usual choice. Nothing about this house is known, so it gets that.
Not known. Three openings across a 30 foot front is the usual way for a house of two rooms. The number is ours, not the paper's.
Not known. Two chimneys, one for each of the two front rooms, is how such houses were laid out. Our guess for this house.

Not known either way. Bare gray boards are our usual for frame buildings when no record tells. And it is backed nearby. St Mary's, the one 1833 church whose outside finish is known, was not painted. The Sauganash's white paint was special enough to be written down.

Not known either way. Bare gray boards are our usual for frame buildings when no record tells. And it is backed nearby. White paint was special enough in Chicago in 1831 to be written down about the Sauganash.

Not known. A jail lets a person in on foot, and nothing else, no horse and no wagon. So it gets a door for people. It is the only kind that fits under this wall. Where the door was, what it was made of, and if it had bars, are not known. They are our usual.
Not known. One floor is usual for a food store this size, and it is how the 1830 plan draws it.

Not known for this building. Long boards that lap over each other were the usual cover for a wood frame house then. Stow's story of logs calls the cover weatherboards. That is the same thing. So both stories end up with the same boards on the outside.
Not known for sure. Long overlapping boards were the usual cover for a frame building of this kind and time.

No record gives a number. Everything told of is on one level: pine benches, a floor of split logs, plastered walls, no tower. Nothing tells of a balcony, stairs or an upper room. A $600 wood church with benches for 200 had one floor. That is a guess from the words, not a count.

Not given as a number. Everything the page tells of is on one level: rough benches for seats, the plainest tables for the altar and pulpit, no plaster. A building 25 by 35 feet that cost about $400 is a box with one floor. Nothing hints at an upper seating area, a stair or an upper room. A guess from the record.

No record says. It is built of sawn wood, not logs. It was a new building on the main corner in 1833, not yet finished that November. There was almost no brick on the south side until 1837. The light kind of frame was first made in Chicago in 1832 and 1833, and the word building does not tell us which. Either way it looks the same.

Neither record says. A log meeting house and school of one room at this time had one floor, as that kind did. Neither record tells of a stair, a loft or an upper room. A small square log building does not fit a second floor.
Not known. Bare wood is our usual choice, and the smaller claim.

Not known for this fort's barracks. Hubbard says the rooms for the officers on the west side were logs. Only the leader's house is called brick, by two records. A list from 1855 calls the officers' rooms wood. So log barracks were usual here then. Our guess is that each building here was wood, but for the leader's house and the store for gunpowder.
Not known for this fort. An order from 1803 for forts like this said blockhouses were to be made of logs, lightly cut. Nothing says the 1816 rebuild did it any other way.
Not known. But rough is known, and a whitewashed building is not a rough one. Bare wood is also our usual choice.
Not known. A log building 16 by 20 feet has one floor, as that kind did. Two floors on that plan would be a tower. A guess from the known size, as close to proof as our number of floors gets.

Not known. A 50 by 25 foot brick house for the leader of the fort, tall enough to be one of the two main buildings in a photo from across the river, had two floors. That is a guess from its size and how it stood out, not from a record.

No record says. A log house split into a schoolroom and a place to live is one floor with two rooms. Nothing tells of stairs or an upstairs room. Our other log buildings of this time are built the same way.

Not known. A book calls it a small log building, 20 feet deep. Two pages say it was split side by side, a post office on one side and a store on the other, not by floors. A log building that deep here in 1835 had one floor. That is a guess from its kind and the record.
No record says. Andreas calls it a wooden building for auctions, one room for one use. One floor fits that. It might have had two, if Bates rented out the top. Nothing we found says.

Not known. Andreas splits the building into rooms, not floors. That is how you tell of a log house with two rooms on one floor. A log house of two floors in Chicago in 1831 would have been worth saying. A guess from the record and the kind, not from a statement.
No record says. Andreas calls it small. A building with two floors would be named for its floors, as he does for Peck's store. So it has one floor. That is a guess from the word he chose.
Not known. Bare, packed earth. No record tells of the ground. A fort far out west in 1835 would not have had stones or gravel here. The town's own streets were mud for ten more years.

Not known. Which kind of frame is not known. A wood frame is our guess, from the time and place alone. Most buildings on the south side in 1834 and 1835 were frame or logs, with no brick building to speak of before 1837. A building big enough to pack in wants open floor, which a frame gives and logs do not. We do not use the name as proof. A bank might be thought to be stone or brick. In Chicago in 1834, it could not have been.
Not known. A wood frame, not logs. A store house wants open floor and wide doors, and most shops on South Water then were frame. Which kind of frame is not known.

No record says. It is built of sawn wood, not logs. A warehouse wants an open floor and wide doors. There was almost no brick on the south side until 1837. The light kind of frame was just being invented in Chicago in 1832 and 1833, the year of this building. So we can't tell which kind of frame it had.

Not known. A wood frame, not logs. It is a shop at the town's main corner. Most buildings on the south side in 1835 were frame or logs, with no brick to speak of before 1837. Which kind of frame cannot be told from any record.

No record says. It is built of sawn wood, not logs. In 1835, new shops on the main street went up in wood frame. There was almost no brick on the south side until 1837. By 1835 people here built with a light kind of frame. This is the building where that is most likely.
Not known. A wood frame, not logs, because this is a shop on the town's main street in 1835. Most new shops then were frame. Which kind of frame is not known.
Not known. A wood frame, not logs. This is a big clothes store on the town's main street in June 1835. Most new shops then were frame. Which kind of frame is not known.
Not known. A wood frame, not logs. Most shops on South Water then were frame, and a food store wants open floor and a wide door. Which kind of frame is not known.
Not known. A wood frame, not logs. Most shops on South Water in the middle 1830s were frame, with logs mostly in older buildings. This shop is not known before 1833. Which kind of frame is not known.
Not known. Logs, for the same reason as the soldiers' rooms. Every building here but the leader's house and the powder house is called wood, when anyone says at all.
Not known. Our usual choice, the same as every work building here. Our guess.

Not known. Two floors, with the upper one sticking out, is what makes a blockhouse. The 1803 order says blockhouses were placed so soldiers could cover the walls from the upper and lower floors. That means two floors.
Not known. Bare wood is our usual choice, and how every work building in this town is done. Paint on an army barn would be the claim.
Nothing tells this building's color. Bare wood is our usual for a frame building when no record says. The Sauganash is the one we paint, because Wau-Bun calls it white.

Nothing is known about the inside. Two rooms is our usual plan, and what 480 square feet on one floor holds. Our note on the sale calls it a small home of two or three rooms. A choice for the kind, not proof.

Nothing is known about its street front. The two uses the records tie to it, a bank and a hog packing floor, are both buildings without shop windows. So we leave off the shop front. That is a guess from its known use, not from a record of how it looked.

Our guess, and marked so. Nothing is known, and there is no reason either way from its kind. A packing house is one tall floor. A bank is a building of two floors, with offices above. The name says one thing and the use says the other. One floor is given because it is the smaller claim.

Nothing is known. One floor is given because it is the smaller claim, and the price fits it. $250 in Chicago in 1834 buys a small cottage, not a house with rooms above. A floor and a half would fit its size too. We do not pick it. Where two answers fit, we take the one that claims less.
Nothing is known. One floor is given because it is the smaller claim. The ad tells of a counter and a stock room, and never a room above. Our guess, and marked so.
Nothing is known. One floor is given because it is the smaller claim. A shipping house with a loft above would be just as likely. Our guess, and marked so.

Nothing says if this house had a porch, and we do not give it one. That is the smaller claim. A porch two floors high is the kind of thing a record would mention. None of the three records about this building does.
Nothing says. Logs, like every other building at this fort. Our guess.

One support, because of how long it is. The other crossing needs none for 8 meters, since an 8 meter log reaches across. That does not work for 12 meters. One support in the middle makes two runs of 6 meters, which fits the same reasoning. Our usual spacing would put two supports in a six meter stream. Saying one keeps the guess small.

One record, and it is from before 1835. It starts on 24 February 1830, the date on the Harrison plan. That plan is the only record we have about this building. It ends on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That is not when it came down. Nothing tells when the fort's outer buildings were torn down. What counts for July 1835 is the middle. Soldiers were here the whole time from June 1832 to the end of 1836. A building drawn in 1830 still stood five years later, unless something says it stopped. Nothing does. With only one record, this is a weaker case than for the wash house.

A slope of 28 degrees, our guess for the roof of two slopes in the 1902 picture. That makes it 1.2 meters high, not the lower cap we had before. The drawing gives the taller roof, not a measured slope, plan, or proof of how it looked in July 1835. The other roof in Andreas's picture does not make a second building.
One chimney that looks like brick is in Gale's picture. It stands near the east end, as pictured. Its place and size are our guess.

Our reading of the 1902 picture, labeled 1836. The pointed end in the picture is the east end. From the north front, it shows two windows and then the door. The end shows two windows on the ground floor and a small one in the loft. All the sizes, which way it faces, and that it was so in July 1835 are our guesses. Andreas's picture shows a different side. We do not claim the two match.
One low roof of two slopes, our guess. No record measures the slope.
One low floor, with a small window up in the loft. We do not claim a half floor where people lived.

One floor, partly built, is our choice for July 1835. It could have been anywhere from nothing to two floors. A notice of 10 June says work had started. Bonnell, years later, tells of it being built, but gives three different years. Martineau tells of it unfinished in June 1836. A book says it opened in the fall of 1836. So it was not done, but we cannot tell how far it was in July. We build one part done floor, with no roof and no hotel inside.

Cameron's picture, made years later, shows one window between the corner and a door off to one side. Where they sit is our guess, moved after we checked our pictures. The drawing's lines do not quite agree. The full match is still open. The side no one sees is our usual.
A house of 6.4 by 4.6 meters. Both sizes and the back are our guess. The picture shows how it looked, but never a plan with sizes.

Our guess for 1835, from a picture. A book says the church had no tower when it was built in 1833. Some time later it got a low open tower and a bell, but no date is given. Moss's print, with no date, shows an open bell tower, a curved pointed cap and a cross. We use that shape for 1835 as our guess. It does not prove the tower was there by July 1835. Its posts, rails, bell, cap and cross have sizes we chose. Tower or no tower in 1835 is our choice, not a dated record.

No street corner left today shows where this building stood. The streets here were laid out in 1833 to 1835, and the point has been built over since. So its place is worked out from where the rivers meet and the shape of the banks. What is known agrees well. One page says the Miller House stood on the point of land between the North Branch and the main river. Wau-Bun says on the north side of the river, near the forks. A book says a store on the north bank at the forks. And the Miller ferry ran across the North Branch between this house and the Wolf Point inn, which puts it on the point. One record puts Miller on the south branch, across from Wolf Point. We treat that as a mistake. It is four against one, and the ferry settles it. We used today's river maps to find the point, and set the house back from both rivers. It could be off by about 20 meters, more along the bank, since the banks have been filled and built over. The front faces south onto the river, from a house facing the river. On a point, the river is on two sides, so it could face the forks instead.

Placed on 9 August 2026. The corner is known. A website and the city's landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market. But the exact spot is our guess, so the grade follows the weaker half. Market Street is today's Wacker Drive, and Lake Street is the same. The old maps fit today's streets well. We found the corner on today's maps, and set the building just inside the south-east corner lot, facing Lake Street. It could be off by about 20 meters. The front faces north, onto Lake Street. The records say it faced the forks to the north-west, so it may have turned more that way. But the lots are square to the streets, so a corner building facing Lake is the safer reading.

Placed on 11 August 2026. One book does not agree with itself about which side of Clark Street it was on. The school pages say twice that it stood on the river bank, just east of Clark Street. The church pages say it was on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle. That is west of Clark, about a block away. We follow the school pages. They are more exact, they say it twice, and they are about this building. The church pages name a meeting place in passing. If the church pages are right, it stood about 110 meters west of where we draw it. We found Clark Street on today's maps, and the 1834 river bank on an old map. The school sits just east of Clark, on the strip of bank by the river. It faces south to the river, our guess. It could be off by 20 meters or more, and the block question is far bigger than that.

Placed from one sentence, not from the plan. The 1830 plan draws no powder house. Hubbard wrote in 1827 that it was brick, about half way between the guard house and the blockhouse. That put the guard house on the west side of the south gate. It is the only way that leaves a gap for the powder house. We put it in the middle of that gap. About half way is all we have. The sentence can be read two ways, which moves it about 4 meters.

Placed from the plan, and backed by two writers. The 1830 plan draws a heavy box at the south-west corner, sticking out past both walls. It is the only part of the fort drawn that way. A book says the blockhouse was in the south-west corner. Hubbard said the same in 1827. Three records, one corner.

No size is known, but two clues pull against each other. Bonnell calls it a small yellow house. Then he says Mrs. Kelsey had all the boarders she could take, and turned him away. So it was small, but full. 8.5 by 6.1 meters is about 28 by 20 feet. It has two front rooms, and rooms under the roof where boarders slept. Every number is our guess. What is not a guess is that it is the smaller of the two houses here. One record calls it small, and calls the other a home.

Every number is our guess. No size is known. 11 by 8 meters is about 36 by 26 feet, a house with two front rooms and a hall. The only clue to its size is who lived here. Bonnell calls it a home, not a house or a cabin. The man who lived here was a doctor, and half of a drug store on South Water Street. So it is given the front of a doctor's house, not a worker's cabin. That is a reason from his trade, not a measure. It is smaller than the houses whose sizes we know, because nothing here is known at all.
Every number is our guess. No size is known. 18 by 26 feet is our size for a wood cottage of two rooms. That is what a merchant builds to rent.
No size is known. 20 by 26 feet is our size for an older log cabin. That is one room and a loft, what a doctor's home and office would be in a town this size. Every number is our guess.
No size is known. 22 by 30 feet is our size for a deep wood cottage. It fits the biggest family we know of here: a wife and five sons, the youngest born in this house. Every number is our guess.

Every number is our guess. No size is known. 22 by 34 feet is a wood building of two floors, with a work room below and an attic where someone lived. That is the least that fits a law office on the ground floor and a bed in the attic.

This is a guess. No record gives a size. 24 by 40 feet is a log boarding house with a hall and two rooms below, and a loft for sleeping above. That is the smallest house that fits a fine boarding house with its keeper, her family and the people who paid to stay. Every number is made up.

Every number is our guess. No size is known. 24 by 18 feet is a school of one room, big enough for the thirty children Watkins wrote his sign-up for. Beware the one size the record does give. It is for a different building. Watkins's first school room, in the fall of 1832, was Colonel Hamilton's horse stable, twelve feet square. That is not this house. A building twelve feet square is not what the book means by the first house built for a school.

Every number is our guess. No size or plan is known. The records give only a kind: a log house used to tan hides. 7 by 5.5 meters is a usual one-room log house of the time. It looks like a house put to work, not a building made for the trade, as the records say. Note what is not built. A tannery is mostly its yard: a mill for bark, pits, big tubs, drying sheds and water. None of that is in the model. We build only the log house the records name. To settle it, look for any record of Miller and Hall's yard, or their ads in the Chicago Democrat.

Every number is our guess, and no record is given. No size is known, and we build the shop at its bigger size. A book says Pierce soon had to make his shop bigger. It gives no date and no size before or after. So this is the shop after it grew, the way it would be in 1835. 9 by 7 meters is about 30 by 23 feet. That is room for a fire, an anvil, a horse to be shod, and the plow work he took up in the spring of 1834. The 9 meters face Lake Street.

This is a guess, but we chose it to fit how much work was done here. In 1833 about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs were packed here by Clybourne, and more by George W. Dole. That much work needs a floor wide enough for several animals, a room to hang them and a yard. So it is about 39 by 30 feet, big for a log building here. The long side runs along the river bank. Every number is made up. We do not build the pens, the stock yard or the tools. We build only the building.

This is a guess. No record gives a size. It is about 17 by 13 feet, the smallest of the three houses here. Every number is made up. Even making it the smallest is a guess about a helper's pay, not something we read.

This is a guess. No record gives a size. It is about 18 by 14 feet, a one-room log house. Every number is made up. The only clue is the word small. Andreas tells of another house for this man too. It was a wood frame house the government built for Caldwell, far to the north. That is a different building, and it is not in the model.

This is a guess. No record gives a size. It is about 20 by 15 feet, a blacksmith shop with one fire. That is room for a forge, an anvil and a horse. Every number is made up. Andreas said McKee had a little shop and few tools. That is our only clue it was small.

Every number is our guess. No size is known. 6.1 by 4.6 meters is about 20 by 15 feet, a log house of one room. Mrs. Susan Callis remembered two rooms in the government house of 1816. This has one fewer. The only clue to size is the word small in the book. That is not a measure. The three houses here get three slightly different sizes, so the row does not look like one building stamped three times. That is our guess too.

This is a guess. No record gives a size. It is about 20 by 16 feet, a small home for one man with a $350-a-year job. Every number is made up. The records give his pay, the light and the tower's height, but no size for any house.

Every number is our guess, and no record is given. No size, shape or plan is known. 7 by 6 meters is about 23 by 20 feet, a one-room store house of the time. The long side runs along the river. The records give a trade, not a building. A store selling food and goods for trade with the Native people names what it sold, not what it was made of. A book's line names the trader and his neighbor, not his building. To settle it, look at Andreas's pages on Wolf Point, or the old pictures of Wolf Point.

This is a guess. No size, shape or plan is known. The record that tells of the business says it gives no building sizes, shapes or plans. It is about 33 by 23 feet, a work shed big enough for a kettle, a floor to cool and shape candles, and an ash bin. The long side runs along the river bank. Every number is made up.

No size is known. Only two words are, and they do not agree. Wau-Bun calls it a small square log building. A website calls it an oblong building. We use square, because Wau-Bun is earlier, and she told of what she saw. The website's is a memory written down further away. But a 7 by 7 meter square is a guess at size wearing a known shape. So the whole shape is marked as our guess, with no record given. 7 meters is about 23 feet, a log building of one room, big enough for ten church members and a school. The fight over its shape hints that there may have been two buildings, one square and one long.

No size, shape or plan is known for this building. The Miller house's shape is known, and only its size is a guess. Here we know neither. Our notes say only that it was south of Wentworth's inn, on the west bank. Its kind, date and look are not known. 8 by 6.5 meters is about 26 by 21 feet, a usual log house of the time. We picked a shape to sit in a row on the river, not one anyone told of. No record is given, because none backs it. To settle it, look at the pages of Andreas's book about Wolf Point, or the picture called Wolf Point in 1830.

No record tells what it was made of or how big it was. 15 by 8 meters is about 50 by 26 feet, a likely town hotel of two floors in 1835. It is sized between the Green Tree, 40 by 25 feet, and the Western Hotel, which is known. Every number is our guess. It is a plain box because no record tells of a plan. To settle it, look at the ads in the Chicago American and Chicago Democrat. Davis put ads in for this house, and hotel ads then often counted rooms and told of the building.

This is a guess. Nothing is known about its size or plan. It is about 40 by 23 feet, one long room big enough for a council meeting and a church service. Those are the two uses the records tell of. Every number is made up. It is a plain box because no record tells of a plan.

No one wrote down what held the bridge up. The branch bridges stood on frames of four heavy logs, because four men who used them said so. Nothing like that exists for this bridge. We first chose boxes of logs filled with stone, our usual kind. The harbor works nearby were being built that way then. That is a reason, not a proof. Now an old picture from 1884 shows big wide bases under the lifting part, and lighter frames under the rest. So the rest stand on four-log frames, our guess. The two big bases are built on their own.
Patched. The wagon tops and tents had come a long way, over hundreds of miles of road.

A plain square box of boards with a pointed cap, in the middle of the roof. No picture shows this barn's cupola. Its shape, place, bare boards and no windows are our guess from one word on the plan, not measured from a picture.
Our usual height, not measured from the drawing.
The chimney top is shorter than our usual, to match the short chimney in Cameron's picture. It is not a measure.
Rooms for the fort's soldiers. The best-known story about it is not about soldiers. In 1827, with the fort empty, families of fur-trade boatmen lived in it. That September it burned.
Rooms for the fort's lower officers. In 1827 there were no soldiers here. Hubbard found Russel Heacock and one more family living in them. That tells us about 1827, not 1835.

Read from how the map is drawn, not from a word on it. The 1830 plan draws two sides of the garden as a zigzag line, and two as plain lines. On old American maps, a zigzag means a rail fence that zigzags. Soldiers with axes and no tools for digging post holes built that kind. This is a guess from how maps were drawn. The map does not say fence.

This is a choice to fit a picture, not a measure. An old drawing of the shore shows a much narrower front than we had before. So the front is now 15 feet wide. The house goes back far enough to keep the same floor space as before. That keeps room for its two known uses, a school and a place to live. The drawing gives no scale and does not prove which building this is. The sizes, the depth and the date of 1835 are all our guess.

Our idea of the picture, not a survey. A print of 1867, labeled 1833, shows the tall house next to a wide, low log part. The building is now a box of 15 by 6 meters: the tall part 9 by 6, and the low log part 6 by 6. Every meter is our guess. No record gives the old sizes or the new ones. That it still looked this way in July 1835 is our guess, not a dated fact.
Our guess. The tall part is 6 meters deep. The low log part next to it is just as deep, and 6 meters wide. The record shows two parts of different heights side by side, not any of these sizes.
Our guess. The tall part is 9 meters wide, not measured from the picture. That leaves 6 meters for the low log part next to it. Where the front openings sit, and the roof's span, are our guess too.

Houses for rent, which no one else shows. A town where a merchant puts an ad for two buildings to let is a town with houses for rent. That is one of the ways 3,265 people fit into 398 homes. There is a trap in the same ad. It has a picture of a building of three floors. That was a stock picture the printer kept, not a picture of anything in Chicago. Nothing about these two buildings' shape comes from it.

Graded again on 9 August 2026, from a weaker guess to a stronger one. No height is known for this building. But two full floors of the usual height is worked out from its kind and how people built. The old grade said no proof, while this same note gave the reasons. 5.5 meters is about 18 feet, two floors of 8 feet with the floors between. The size is still not sure. What we know is that it was about this tall, not exactly 5.5 meters.

Our size, not measured from Gifford's drawing. The box stays 50 by 30 feet, so the three floors and shutters in the picture stay the same. A book of 1902 does give 20 by 30, likely feet, in a walk set in 1835. So we no longer say no size is known. That smaller size, with two floors, is kept as another version. Neither record proves when it was made bigger, or how it looked on 1 July 1835. Our bigger size is still our guess. Gifford's picture sets the floors, windows and shutters we see.
Raised steps can be seen at both doors in the picture. Their sizes, steps and side rails are our guess. The doors no one sees get the same. Four doors, and the sizes of their steps, are not known.

The chimney rises 0.65 meters above the roof top, lower than our usual. Braunhold draws a short chimney that can be seen above the small roof. The exact height is our first guess, not a measure. We still need to check it against the picture.
The window's width is our guess from Cameron's drawing, made wider after the first check. He shows where things are, not how big.

Our first guess at the height of the tall windows in Braunhold's print. It makes them twice as tall as wide, not almost square as before. The print shows the taller shape, but gives no size. The back window, which no one sees, gets the same height. That side is our guess.

Our first guess at the width of the narrow tall windows in Braunhold's print. The picture shows they were tall and narrow, but gives no size. 0.7 meters is our choice for now, until we check it against the picture. Not a known size.

The keeper's house stands 7.8 meters east of the jail, and a little north of it. Both face north, our choice. That puts the keeper's house on the left and the jail yard on the right, as in Gale's picture. None of these numbers is measured from the print. The house and jail stay in the public square. No street or lot moves.

How the stone is built. The rows are about 0.3 meters tall, a little uneven, with chipped corners. The five stone colors are our guess. No picture shows the real stone, its kind or its color. The pictures can't tell us if it was bare stone or painted white.

How the lantern room is built. The glass is almost clear, with a dark edge at the bottom and a round top. It has 12 thin posts, and the walkway has 16. These choices are shaped by the pictures, but they are not real counts or colors.

Open with no roof is our choice for 1 July 1835. The 10 June notice says work had started, but not when the roof went on. The later facts do not prove there was no roof in July either. A later print shows a finished roof and a little tower, but it is from after 1836. It cannot tell us how far the work was in July.

Our guess at the width of the small chimney through the roof, in Braunhold's print. The picture shows a narrow chimney on this small roof, not a measured size. 0.55 meters is our choice for now. Its square shape and plain sides are our usual, not claims that the picture is fully copied.

How the tower's height is split. The walkway is about 8.7 meters up, and the top part starts at 11 meters. The very top is about 12.8 meters. The long numbers are not exact history. 40 feet is the round number in the record, and no one knows just what was measured.

This is a test width of about 3 meters, not a measure. The middle and the place stay the same as before. The narrowing of the tower and the size of the walkway are our guess. The record's 40 feet still is not settled.

We keep this note on a view we do not use, so it stays in sight. W. H. Stow said the Green Tree was first made of logs, and covered in boards years later. We take that as wrong, for the reasons in the note on how it was built. If he is right, it is logs under boards, not a wood frame. That changes the walls, but not the shape, plan or place.
The roof slopes at 35 degrees, our guess. It fits the steep front roof in an old drawing, and how log roofs were built. The drawing is tiny and does not measure the slope.

The tall part keeps its 38 degree roof, our guess. The low part has its own lower roof, a 25 degree guess. The chimney on the tall part sits under the same roof slope. The roof ends and the chimney's place moved a little where the two parts join. The real ends and places are not measured, and neither change is a new claim about history.

Sawn boards, not split logs. This is the first record where we use that. The bridges on the branches had floors of split logs, what a crew lays without a saw. This bridge was different. Norton began cutting the lumber in the winter of 1833, and spent three months building it, with a part that lifted. A ship's carpenter does not build that from rough split wood. So the boards are narrow and even. But cutting the lumber could mean cutting trees, not sawing boards. So it is a guess.

Mason and Co. put an ad in the Chicago Democrat, and the ad ran for a year. The ad of 26 November 1833 says they are blacksmiths on Main Street, nearly across from Graves' inn. The and Co. means more than one man worked there. Eleven printings of the ad are read, the last on 10 December 1834. So the shop is known to have run thirteen months. A working blacksmith in a town growing ten times over is far more likely to have kept going than to have shut. Partway through, the ad changes how it tells where the shop is. The note on its place tells about that.

Six feet, and the reason is better than the number. A book prints a paper signed by Caton, Bates, Cleaver and Noble. It says both were wagon bridges, about six feet above the water, so teams passed under them on the ice. The space under it was not for the builders' ease. It was the winter road under the deck, told by four men who used the crossing. It also does the most harm to the idea that it was a raft. A floating deck has no space under it, and nothing passes under it on the ice.

Six feet, borrowed from the bridges nearby, and marked as borrowed. No record says how high this bridge stood over the water. The only number we have is from 1883, when old settlers said the two bridges on the branches stood about six feet up. Two things fit. The bridges were built within two years of each other, for the same town. And a bridge that opened sixty feet for boats could not be high, or it would not need to open. One thing does not fit. This river carried tall-masted ships, so its bridge had more reason to be high. We keep six feet because it is the only number we have.
The same reason as the officers' rooms. Porches facing the parade ground are known for the first fort, but for no building in this one. A plain front is a claim the visitor sees.
Our guess. Sawn boards nailed up and down, the same as the packing house at the other end.

Sawn boards nailed up and down. Chicago had sawn wood by 1834, and this is a building made for the work, not a settler's cabin. So boards, not logs. Our guess. Nothing says how any building here was built.

Sawn boards nailed up and down. Elston's works was a business that put ads in the town paper, not a settler's shed. So it has boards, not logs. That is a guess about the business, not from a record. Made up.

Shutters can be seen around the windows in Gifford's picture. Green is our chosen color. The black and white picture gives no color. Their size, how far they open and their parts are our guess. No slats are claimed.

Father St. Cyr picked the lot in 1833. The same page says Father O'Meara took his place only after 1837. So he led the church through all these years. It is marked as our guess, because the page tells when he came and when he was replaced, not who was in charge on any one day in 1835.
Stow is known as the man who built and ran the hotel. That the stable behind it was his follows from its being part of the house. It is not said on its own. No stable hand is named.

Ten feet, and for once it is said twice. The old settlers' paper of 1883 says these bridges were about ten feet wide, with no railings for the first few years. Cleaver said in the Tribune ten years later that these bridges were ten feet wide. Both are about both river bridges. So this crossing's width is proof, not a guess from the bridge next to it. Cleaver signed the first and gave the second, so it is one man backed by three. We record it as exactly 3.048 meters, ten feet. The same paper says the North Branch bridge was ten or twelve feet wide. This one does not take that, since it was said of the other bridge.

Ten feet, from Charles Cleaver, for both bridges over the river's branches. It is the only size of any building here that a record really gives. Here is why we trust it. Cleaver used this bridge and drove a team across it. A width is the kind of number someone who used a narrow bridge remembers. We record it as exactly 3.048 meters, which is ten feet.

How this bridge looked in 1835, after it changed. A book says the 1832 bridge was made of long logs and fit only for people on foot. Even in the summer of 1833 it was useless for wagons. But six and a half weeks after the day we show, hundreds of people crossed it in a parade, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. So it was rebuilt or made wider between 1833 and 1835. No record says how. Four logs under a full deck is the later, stronger reading. We chose it because the day is 1 July 1835, and the proof for 1835 is a crowd on it. The 1832 walkway, two logs and a board, would be right for a scene of 1833.

Its use in 1835 is known, which we did not expect. A book puts George Davis teaching in the Presbyterian church in 1835. Then it says John Watkins was then teaching a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building put up by Colonels Hamilton and Owen. So it was a public school in the year we show. But that is the year, not the day. The book says Watkins taught as late as 1835, but no one knows when he stopped. So it cannot be tied to 1 July.

The known traffic is the reason, and also why this is not a wagon door. The record says wagons were driven into the yard, the yard into which the trains were driven, and horses went in the stable. So what goes through this building's door is a horse led by hand. That is a stable door, 1.35 meters wide. A wagon door 2.9 meters wide would quietly move the wagons indoors. There is another real answer. A wagon house at an inn for drivers often had a cart bay at one end. Nothing rules it out, and nothing says so. So the smaller door is recorded.

The best known wall height we have, because someone told how high a ceiling was. A guest wrote that seven and a half feet was rather low for an inn's ceiling. Two floors at 7 and a half feet is 15 feet. Add the floors between, and it is about 16 and a half feet, or 5 meters, to the roof. The 7 and a half feet is known. The rest is our guess.

The year it was built is argued, 1834 or 1835, and we settle it here. But the reason matters, because the two dates mean different things for this scene. A website tells of W. H. Stow, who came to Chicago about 1833. He said of his own hotel that it was built in 1834. A list of hotels says it opened in 1835. We use 1834, because it is the builder's own word about his own building. It comes with the same details that give its sizes and yard. The list gives one line, no date of its own, and gets the size wrong. If 1835 were right, the hotel might have been unfinished on 1 July 1835. But showing that would mean making up a month and how far it was built, which no record gives. One finished stage on the better date claims less. If 1835 is ever proved, we can split it then. The dates end in 1840, after the last record of it being run. That is not when it came down. No record gives that.

We know the year it was built, but not the month, so we start at the beginning of 1827. A book says Archibald Clybourne built a log butcher house in 1827, to kill cattle for the soldiers at Fort Dearborn. We know it still worked in 1833. That year he packed about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs here. So it was busy less than two years before July 1835. The record ends at the end of 1835. By 1883 a newer wood one stood here, falling apart from age. So the log one came down some time between 1835 and 1883.

It is a choice for the kind, not proof about this building. The building is known. This detail is not. A record places this building and says what it was. But nothing records this size or detail. So it is what a building of this kind was usually like. It is our guess, not because the building is in doubt, which it is not. Only this number is.

The building is known, but this detail is not. A record places the building and says what it was. Nothing tells this number, so we use what a building of this kind was usually like. The building is not in doubt. Only this number is.

So it is what a building of this kind was usually like. It is our guess, not because the building is in doubt, which it is not. Only this number is.

The dates are the shop's, not the building's. A book lists Jim Kinzie's store, Peck's, Harmon's and Loomis's on South Water Street by 1833. It also says J. H. Kinzie put ads in the paper in 1834 as a shipper. The dates start in 1833 and end with the year. Nothing dates the building. A word of warning about the name. The book's Jim Kinzie is James Kinzie, who kept two inns on the west bank. The 1834 ads are John H. Kinzie's. Which brother owned the store, or both at different times, is not settled. Our name for it follows the book's ad.

The deck, and not one of its numbers comes from a record. It is 12 meters long and 3 meters wide. Its length is sized to the stream, like the other two crossings. There are 6.65 meters of open water, with dry ground left at both ends. It is the width that matters most. It is the smallest of the three, and that is the reason for it. Cleaver's ten feet is for the two river bridges, and is only a guide here. 3 meters is a little under it. This crossing carries North Water Street, a quiet street with a narrow track. South Water is much wider, so its crossing is wider. A crossing wider than its road needs would be a claim, and nothing backs one. This is not a river bridge. The two river bridges are 72 and 56 meters long. This crosses a six meter backwater.

The end of this range is a limit, not a date. Juliette Kinzie lived inside the fort in 1831. She wrote that it was fenced in by high posts. The 1830 plan draws them too. In 1850 Robert Fergus wrote that a rough board fence, whitewashed, about 6 feet high, ran round the fort, and the posts had been taken away. Nothing tells when they came down. On 1 July 1835 there were soldiers in the fort, and the posts stood. No one pulls down a fort's wall with soldiers inside it.

Its outer size is known, but not its plan. The record says the front was about forty feet and the wing sixty feet, in an L shape. 40 feet is 12.19 meters and 60 feet is 18.29 meters. That is the box around our shape, exactly. The record does not say how wide each arm was. So 7 meters, about 23 feet, is our guess, enough for a room and a hall. It is the narrowest that makes an L, not a solid block. The record's own word is about. Not everyone agrees. The list of hotels calls the Western a small building. That does not fit a 40 by 60 foot L with two floors. We prefer the website's sizes. They come with the builder's story, and with the yard and stable. The list gives no sizes at all, so small is a feeling, not a measure. The stable and yard are known, but are not in this shape.

The flag is known, and its pattern comes from the law. A book says this pole flew a worn flag. A fort flew the national flag. No record says how many stars. A law of 1818 adds a star on the 4th of July after a new state joins. Missouri made 24 stars on 4 July 1822. Arkansas made 25 only on 4 July 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the flag had 24 stars and 13 stripes. How the stars were laid out, four rows of six, the flag's size and its wear are our guess.

The start date is the ad's, not the building's, and two papers print it. The Chicago Democrat ran it on 10 June 1835, and the Chicago American on 13 June. The Democrat's came first, so its date is the start. Both say he is now opening his goods here. So the shop opens in the second week of June 1835. The building must be older than the shop, but no record dates it. What we know is that a clothes and boot store was open on South Water Street three weeks before the day we show. The end is just the end of the year. The papers we have run to August 1835, and nothing says when Holbrook left.

There were soldiers here on 1 July 1835, and we checked it. A book gives the order. The soldiers left in 1823. They came back in October 1828. They left for Green Bay in May 1831. In June 1832 soldiers came again, and they stayed until 29 December 1836. Wilcox was in charge until December 1833 and again from September 1835. Others led in between. A list fills that gap with Major John Greene. How many soldiers there were in 1835 is not known. A book says two groups in 1833, and nothing later. So no number is given. The soldiers are why the gates are shut, and why the fort is kept up, not falling down.

Its name tells what it was, and every record uses it. A United States factory was the country's own trading house. It is where trade with the Native people was done for the government. All three records name it so. The plan names it the U.S. Factor's House. Hubbard says a Mr. Jouett, the factor, lived in it. Hurlbut says the American Fur Company bought it from the United States. What went on inside in 1835 is not claimed. The trading houses were shut in 1822, the same year Hurlbut says it was sold. By 1835 this was a private house that used to be a trading house. Nothing we have says if any trade still went on in it.

This is one of the most useful buildings we found. In 1835 there were 3,265 people and only 398 homes, and boarding houses held the rest. Andreas says the houses of 1834 were always full. Full sometimes meant three in a bed, with more people on the floor. New settlers lived in their covered wagons outside. Andreas says this house was made of logs. That makes it one of the few log buildings in the middle of town.

The two records give his first letter two ways, and we do not pick one. A book says H. Jones. The 1833 ad says B. Jones. An ad is the man's own word on his own name, and should win. But the old page is damaged, and B and H are easy to mix up in big print of that time. The typed copy of that paper has other mistakes too. So we keep Jones, but not the letter. Both are kept in the record.

The label tells what it was not. Out Buildings means not the barn, not the shop and not the wash house. The plan names those three on their own, to the north. It says nothing about what went on inside. A fort's out buildings were toilets, wood sheds, stores and pens. Which this was is not on the map, and we do not guess.

It is only 2 meters inside the edge of that land. That is closer than our map can be trusted, so the grade drops one step. The land is right only if our drawn survey line is right. What this note claims, and what it does not. It claims that this building stands on land in the state's book of land sales. This man bought the land from the government on this date. It does not claim he still owned it on 1 July 1835, or lived here, or ever stood on it. A sale is only a sale. The book's only word on where he lived names a county. The land survey lines are worked out, not traced. They are carried from the one survey corner at State and Madison, in squares of one mile.

Our margin is only 8 meters. Our map lines could be off by more than that, so we trust this less. What this row claims: a state record of land sales says this man bought the land where this building stands, on this date. What it does not claim: that he still owned it in 1835, lived here, or ever stood on it. A sale is just a sale. Our land lines are drawn from one known corner, not traced from old maps.

Our closest thing to a known wall for any shed here, but still a guess. Andreas calls it the old cabin, without the word log. But every building written about here before 1820 was made of logs. Andreas found a few run-down log huts with bark roofs in 1816. McKee said all the houses he found in 1823 were logs. No sawn boards came to Chicago until the mills of 1832 and 1833. So a cabin here before 1817 was made of logs. We call it a guess, not a fact, because that line is what this project is built on.

The one thing told about this building, and it is plain: a frame building of two floors. It is why this record exists at all. A store of two floors was worth noting when Lake Street was still mostly cabins and mud. The line calls it the first of its kind. A warning goes with every known fact here. The claim is in a note with no author, added at the foot of a page of maps on a website. Our own notes call it the weakest text in that set, never to rank above Andreas. We use it because it is plain, and the only place this building is found, not because it is strong.

When it opened is in doubt by ten weeks. The man who built it and the man who wrote the book disagree. Nelson R. Norton, a ship's carpenter, wrote that he came in November 1833, began the drawbridge in March 1834, and thought it was done by 1 June. The book says he was wrong, since a paper says the town accepted it in August. We start on 1 August 1834, the later date, when it surely stood. Either way it stood long before July 1835. The end is well known: in July 1839 the town ordered it taken away. Before dawn the next morning a big crowd chopped it to pieces. Our August date comes from an 1834 paper we have not seen ourselves.
The town set a price for keeping a horse, so horses were kept. A horse kept overnight is led in and out. So the stable gets our horse door, 1.35 meters wide.

The priced service is the reason. The county's order of 1831 says a horse could be fed and kept overnight at a licensed Chicago inn, for a set price. A horse that is kept is led in and out. A stable door, 1.35 meters wide, allows that. A door for people would make this a feed store. Then the known service would happen outside, and the building would make no sense.

One record, not two. That is how this one differs from the two next to it. Only the plan names a shop here. Hubbard walks the same ground and does not name it. It starts on 24 February 1830, the date on the plan. It ends on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That is not when it came down. Nothing tells when the fort's outer buildings were torn down. What counts for July 1835 is the middle. Soldiers were here the whole time from June 1832 to the end of 1836. A building drawn in 1830 still stood five years later, unless something says it stopped. Nothing does.

Two records hold this range, and both are from before 1835. It starts on 24 February 1830, the date on the Harrison plan, the first record that shows this building. It ends on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That is not when it came down. Nothing tells when the fort's outer buildings were torn down. What counts for July 1835 is the middle. Soldiers were here the whole time from June 1832 to the end of 1836. A building the fort's own planner drew in 1830 still stood five years later, unless something says it stopped. Nothing does.

Two records tell of it, and both are from before 1835. It starts on 24 February 1830, the date on the Harrison plan. Hubbard tells of the land round the fort in the late 1820s, which puts it earlier, but with no date. It ends on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That is not when it came down. Nothing tells when the fort's outer buildings were torn down. What counts for July 1835 is the middle. Soldiers were here the whole time from June 1832 to the end of 1836. These dates are the fort's, not this building's. No record dates any one building inside Fort Dearborn. We start with the rebuilding in 1816, when soldiers came back about June. We end when the main buildings were torn down in the summer of 1856. What shows it in 1835: this building is on the 1830 plan, and a man named Hubbard saw it on his walk around inside in 1827. Soldiers were at the fort from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

These dates are the fort's, not this one building's. No record dates a building inside the fort. We start with the rebuilding in 1816. We end in the summer of 1856, when the main buildings were torn down. What counts is the middle. Soldiers were at the fort from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

What this note claims, and what it does not. It claims that this building stands on land in the state's book of land sales. This man bought the land from the government on this date. It does not claim he still owned it on 1 July 1835, or lived here, or ever stood on it. A sale is only a sale. The book's only word on where he lived names a county. The land survey lines are worked out, not traced. They are carried from the one survey corner at State and Madison, in squares of one mile.
