Two records come before and after July 1835, and neither names that date. Before: a book says that in 1834 church was held in a few places. One was Billy Caldwell's log council house. After: a paper of 18 August 1835 says the crowd for the last war dance met at the Council House on the north side of the river. A building in use in 1834 and in August 1835 stood in between, unless something took it down. But we treat the two as one building. Neither record says so. If they are two, our shape comes from one and our place from the other. We start on 1 January 1834 and end at the end of 1835.

We know the season, but not the day. Andreas says that in the spring of 1833 Tyler K. Blodgett started a brickyard on the North Side. Henry S. Lampman worked for him, the first brick-maker in the city. We start it on 1 March 1833, the usual start of spring. Bricks were made in summer, so 1833 was the yard's first season. That it still ran in 1835 is a guess, but a good one. A brick hotel went up in 1835, so someone was still making bricks. The record ends at the end of 1835.
The second barber. It is the owner's own example of what these made-up buildings are for. The smallest shop roof on this land, on the street with the inns.

The record gives a word, and we need a number. Kinzie says high posts, and no one else says anything. 3.7 meters is twelve feet, the usual height for a fort's fence like this. It is a guess with a number on it. The height you see is our math, not proof.

A book gives two years, and we take the later one. Andreas says John Bates put up a wooden building in 1833 or 1834, as a room for auctions. So we start it at the beginning of 1834. Either year is fine for 1835. Other records show Bates in town then. He sold land at an auction in 1833, and he helped run the post office. No record tells what became of the building, so we end it at 1835.

The start date depends on which building this is. That is the same question as where it stood. Wau-Bun tells of the log school house at Wolf Point in 1831. The first Methodist group formed on 14 June 1831, with ten people, in a log cabin. So 1831 is the start, by our reading. By the other reading, the building of 1835 is a cabin the group built in 1834 on the other bank. Then these dates start three years too early. The end is firmer. In 1838 the group floated the cabin across the river, and rolled it on logs to Washington and Clark. That ends this stage wherever it began. It is marked as our guess, since the start rests on the 1835 building being the 1831 one.

The start is known to the day, but it is the newspaper's date, not the building's. T. O. Davis started the Chicago American on 8 June 1835. It came out on Saturday mornings. Its office was on Water Street, near the drawbridge. So on 1 July 1835 the paper was 23 days old. That is why this record exists: in July 1835 Chicago had two newspapers, and one was three weeks old. The building must be older than the paper, but no record dates it. The paper went on long after 1835, but from a different place by 1839. No record follows this building.

The start is known to the day, which is rare here. A book says that on 8 October 1833, a young man named Asahel Pierce came to Chicago from Vermont. He began to build a blacksmith shop on Lake Street, at the corner of Canal. The dates start then, when building began, not when the shop was working. Nothing says how long it took. A small board shop takes weeks. The end is our guess. Nothing follows the building after 1834, and the dates end with 1835. But that it lasted is better backed than most here. The book says Pierce did the iron work for the first coach line from Chicago to St Louis in January 1834. That spring he began making the old Bull plow, with a wood blade. A business growing does not close. Pierce was still known in Chicago years later, a city leader in 1843 and 1844, with two streets named after him.

The start is the date someone wrote about the place, not the date it was built. Andreas's list is from about 1830, and the book Wau-Bun's from 1831. A list of agency workers from 1830 and 1831 names the job of striker, a blacksmith's helper. The end is the least we can claim. No record tells when this building went up or came down.

The start is the date someone wrote about the place, not the date it was built. Andreas wrote about the town around 1830, and the book Wau-Bun about 1831. Nothing says when these buildings went up, so we start at the first of the two. The end is the least we can claim. In 1835 the agency still owed the Potawatomi a blacksmith, and it still had workers. So we think the houses around it still stood. No record tells what became of this one.

It starts on the first date a paper of the time puts the shop in Chicago. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 has an ad for B. Jones's food store. That proves a Jones shop was open in town that day. A book also lists a food store and shipping shop by H. Jones in 1834. That tells about a business, not a building. Nothing dates the building, and the dates end with the year.

The start is the first date a record from the time shows this building. Its own renter says so. The first Chicago Democrat came out on 26 November 1833. It says it is printed in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets. A paper that says where it is printed, on that same day, is as good a record as we have. The house is older than that. A book says it was not done in November 1833, so it was going up that year. The paper came out all through 1835, but no record follows the house. The end date is just where our record stops.

It starts on the first date a record puts the shop in business. That is not when the building went up, and we do not say it is. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 has an ad for C. and I. Harmon, dated 18 November. It sells cloth, dishes, tools, food and drink, and leather and saddles for others. So a Harmon store was open in Chicago then, just weeks after the town got a paper. A book also lists Harmon's with other stores on South Water Street by 1833. Neither dates the building. A later page tells of a three-floor building at Clark and South Water, with a paper on its top floor in 1839. If that was the 1835 building, or one before it on the same lot, is not known. The dates end with the year, not because it was torn down.

The street is known, and nothing else. On Lake Street is all the record says: no cross street, no side, no block. It sits on the south side of Lake Street, west of Clark, in the first free spot our rule found. The place is our guess on a known street, and is graded so.

Its use is known, but the camp is our drawing. The American of 13 June 1835 says the docks were covered with men, women and children just off the boats. They would have stayed out under the sky on the docks. Some put up tents right where they landed. The paper does not say where on the river front, and this is one stretch of it. So it is our guess, not a record.

The plan says Shop and nothing more. A fort this size had a blacksmith and often a carpenter. It would be easy to write either one here. We do not, because the plan says only shop. A trade would be us making up who worked in it. What we have is a workshop on the fort's outer ground. Which shop is still a question, for whoever finds the fort's papers.

The year is known, but not the month. So the dates start on 1 January 1831, not on a build day. A book says that in 1831, John Miller built a log house near his brother's inn and used it to tan hides. It was Chicago's first known factory. Another book says John Miller, brother of Samuel, came in 1831 and ran a tannery just north of Miller's inn. The end is the least we can say, not its fate. Nothing follows this building after it opened. The book adds a partner, Benjamin Hall, a tanner who came in 1832. Then the trade drops out of the record. Samuel Miller sold the inn and moved away after his wife died in 1832. So the tannery lasting to 1835 rests on our usual reason: a building stands until something says it did not. So it is marked as our guess.

The year is known, but not the month. And the man who taught there did not remember it the same way. A book says that, by Mr. Wells's report, two men built a house on the north bank, just east of Clark Street. Mr. Watkins kept his school in it. It was the first house built for a school in Chicago. But the book says Mr. Watkins did not remember it so. Forty pages on, the same book says it as fact, and gives 1833. A third page backs a school there too. Jesse Walker held his first church meeting in the Watkins school house, on North Water Street. So a Watkins school house stood near Clark in 1834, whoever built it. The dates start on 1 January 1833 and end with 1835. Watkins taught as late as 1835, but no one knows when he stopped.

The year is known, but not the month. A book says that in 1834, Oliver Newberry and George Dole had a meat plant built on the South Branch. About three hundred cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed there that year. So the dates start in 1834, since no month is given. Packing is winter work, so the plant was likely up by fall, not January. That it lasted to 1 July 1835 is our usual guess, not known. Nothing follows it past its first season. But a plant made for the work, that handled 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in its first year, was not left empty in eighteen months. The firm kept trading in Chicago for years. The dates end with 1835.

A book gives the year twice, but not the month. It says Mr. Beaubien built a new house on the corner of Wells and Lake streets. In August 1834 Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took it over as a hotel and named it the Exchange Coffee House. So it was done and open by August 1834, eleven months before July 1835. We start on 1 January 1834, the first day that year allows. Whatever month it went up, it was open in 1835. The Murphys stayed until 1836. We end where the record stops, not when it came down. A list from 1845 names a hotel on the same corner. It may be the same house or may not.

These dates come from the book's account, not the flagpole's life. Its chapter on Chicago from 1833 to 1837 tells what a visitor saw in those four years, and the flagpole line is in it. Nothing says when the pole went up or came down. So the dates are the book's limits, not the pole's. July 1835 sits well inside. We did not end it on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That dates the soldiers, not the pole, and the buildings stood until the 1850s.

To let, and the renter is not named. The ad shows houses for rent, and nobody in them. So no family is placed in this building, on purpose. To let honestly means a building whose renter we cannot name.

The base sticks out sideways, our guess. The full 1884 picture shows the wide base sticking out toward the front of the view, not just along the bridge. So we moved it 1 meter that way, and kept both tall posts standing on it. This is a test of how it looks. No real place, shore or width is moved or measured from the drawing.

Two readings that do not agree, and we take the one in words. The 1855 list says the officers' rooms were wood, about 30 by 60 feet. That is the shape here. The 1830 plan draws this side about 30 feet deep and about 80 feet long. So the two agree on depth, but not on length. The words win. The scale that would overrule them was set from the same list, so using it would go in a circle. Our building is about 6 meters shorter than the plan draws it. If the plan is right, the room was 80 feet long. If the list is right, it was 60. Nothing settles it.

The 1830 plan names a Shop on the fort's outer ground, between the fort and the lake, south of the wash house. It does not say whose shop. It is the fort's because it stands on the fort's land, with the fort's other named buildings. Which trade worked in it is not claimed. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the fort's work buildings were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

The plan names it Out Buildings and draws it on the fort's ground, south of the fence. It does not say whose it was. It is the fort's because it stands on the fort's land. What went on inside is not claimed. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the fort's work buildings were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

The Beaubiens owned it until 1834. A list of hotels gives Davis in 1835 as the man running it. He may be the John Davis who ran the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien had moved on by the day we show. He built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. Who ran it in 1835 is a lead, not a settled fact.

An old print of the harbor shows a round top, a point on top, an open lantern room and a railing. That print is from about 1838, and we use it for 1835. That is a guess that it did not change. The shapes, the curve of the top, how many parts there are and the colors are our guess. The mirrors are not built.

The Clybourne family lived here and killed animals for meat here. A book says Jonas lived a few miles up the North Branch. It says Jonas and his son were the town's first butchers. They sold meat to the fort. So the cabins were a farm that raised animals for meat, not town houses. That is a guess from the family's work. No record says who lived here on 1 July 1835. The son had his own bigger house from 1829. So no one is placed here.

Gifford's picture shows a striped flag on the roof, with a box in the corner. A United States flag is our reading. The stars cannot be counted. For 1 July 1835, our flag of 24 stars and 13 stripes is right for that year, by the flag law of 1818. Its layout is our guess for this hotel. The black and white picture shows no color or stars. It stops on 3 July 1836, before the flag got its 25th star.

Moss's print shows one chimney near the far end of the roof, away from the bell tower. So the chimney moves near that end. How far from the end is our guess, not measured. The chimney's size stays the same. The near end in the picture is left blank, and so is the far end no one sees.
Our guess. The front wall faces south, onto the yard between this shed and the tannery.
The front faces west, onto the yard between this shed and the works it serves. Made up.
Our guess. The side wall faces north, onto the cart yard between this building and the packing house it serves.

Our guess, like the building. The side wall faces north, onto the cart yard between this building and the plant. That is the only side with a yard. West is the river and the landing. East is a small strip and then Market Street. South is the next building.
Our guess. The side wall faces north, onto the cart yard between this shed and the salt house.

The ad names the trade at the top: hats, clothes, boots and shoes, sold in bulk and one at a time. It tells of goods kept in stock and added to all season. It is a store, as the ad says, not our guess.

The brick shows as bare brick. It is our guess, since nothing tells of the outside of this building at any time. Bare brick is the usual finish. Plaster or whitewash is not ruled out, but it would be odd on an unfinished building.
Our guess. Our usual for a roof of two slopes.
The box's roof edge is 1 meter above the roof top. Its bottom sits a little into the main roof, so there are no gaps. Both the height and the joint are our guess.

What it was first built for is known: a fur company's trading house. What it was used for in 1835 is our guess. A book says Beaubien built a new home and a small trading post next to it. So the old trading house no longer did one of those jobs by 1835, but the book does not say which. We record it as both, since nothing says it stopped being either.

The 1867 print shows a short chimney coming up through the top of the tall part's roof. Its place, width and height are our guesses, not measures. The main roof keeps its 38 degree slope. The low part still has two chimneys, from our guess. The other pictures are not clear enough to say they were not there. No July 1835 detail is known. Our check found the chimney top a little too short, under 18 inches. So it was made 1 centimeter taller. The record does not measure it.

The 1867 drawing, made years later and set in 1833, shows the low log front next to the tall part of two floors. So the tall part stands beside the low part. Our old note said the tall part stood in front of the cabin, from the words facing the river. But those words tell which way it faced, not where it stood. The old note mixed that up. The side by side shape comes from the picture. Its exact sizes, and that it was so in July 1835, are graded on their own. It still faces the river.

Our list has no word for an animal shed. Stable is the closest. Its real use, holding animals before the kill and the plant's work oxen, is in its name and in this note. A meat plant that took 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in a season kept them somewhere first. The plant's own record says the pens are outside its walls. This is the roofed part. The pens are a fence line, and we build buildings. No one is placed in it, and no animal is drawn.
The color of packed ground. No record tells of it. We give it so it is not the color of wood.

The church group began in June 1833 under the Rev. Jeremiah Porter. He came that May and slept in the unfinished loft of Peck's store. No record names the minister here on 1 July 1835. So we name the church group, not a person.
A barrel maker's shop. The meat packing trade needed barrels. It is on South Water, near the shipping houses and the store houses that used its barrels.
The open ground where soldiers line up. It is built as ground worn bare and packed, raised 6 centimeters. That is all we claim about it.

Our guess. Our sizes for a freight shed put the roof edge at 10 to 13 feet, and this is 11.2 feet, inside that. It is the same as the shed next to it, which has the same shape. Our rule is that the smallest plan gets the lowest height, and these two plans are the same.
Our list says boards nailed up and down for a freight shed, with gaps between. Our guess either way. Nothing says how any building on this bank was built.

Our list says boards nailed up and down for a freight shed. This one is logs instead. One of the owner's pictures, and the town's own buildings, make logs usual on the north side in 1835. It also breaks up the row. Four sheds built the same would claim they were built together, and nothing backs that. Our guess either way. Nothing says how any building on this bank was built.

The 1902 picture shows one tall window with what look like bars, in the log end next to the keeper's house. It is on the east end, toward the keeper's house. It is a dark opening with three bars up and one across. Its size, its bars, what it was made of, and that it was there in July 1835 are our guesses. It does not mean there was a second floor or hay loft.

A picture from 1902, labeled 1836, shows a log building with a roof of two slopes, behind a fence of posts. We use that roof now, not the flat one from an earlier note. A picture in Andreas's 1884 book shows a pointed roof that slopes on all sides. We keep that as a place where the two pictures do not agree. Using the 1902 picture for July 1835 is our choice. It does not claim the picture shows July.

Our guess, like the building. The door faces north, onto the yard between this shed and the one next to it. So the two sheds' doors face each other across the yard. Streets run at both ends of the building, so the door could not go there. The south wall faces away from the only way in.
Our guess. The door faces the river street, the side with the traffic and the bridge. This building is turned to face the street, so its front is the river side.

Our notes put this building with Newberry and Dole's, as one of two store houses on the river with docks. That makes it a shipping house by being next to one, not because a record says so. No record says what Kinzie and Hunter shipped. A book says a firm of Kinzie, Hunter and Co. sold wood in the middle 1830s. So a wood yard, not a store house, is another real answer. We record it as our guess, and name the other one.

Our notes say log cabins, but do not say where that came from. A book twice says the family's butcher house on the same land was made of logs. Every settler home on the river's branches in the 1820s that any record tells of was logs. So logs is a guess from the houses nearby and the family's other building. If we ever find where our note came from, this becomes a fact.

An old note guessed long boards from the words partly sided. The 1867 print shows more for the tall part: logs on the lower floor, and boards running up and down on the upper floor and pointed end. We build that now. The first cabin is still logs. The board sizes and the sides no one sees are our guesses. A picture made years later does not settle how it looked in July 1835.
The business names itself in its own ad. That is the best kind of proof here. Who else was a partner, and whether anyone worked here on 1 July 1835, are not known.

The first Catholic church in Chicago. It was in use from October 1833. The first mass was on 5 May 1833. It was said in a different place, a small log cabin twelve feet square. That cabin was Mark Beaubien's. It is not this building.

The fort's one blockhouse, at the south-west corner, guarding the south and west walls. It stayed on as a landmark after the fort. Wentworth says that when the fort's land was sold in 1839, the land where the blockhouse stood was kept.
The frame went up in August 1833, and the church was in use by October.
The fort's store for gunpowder. That it was brick is the one thing about it that is known two ways. Its size, height and roof are our guess.

The fort's garden for fruit and vegetables. The 1830 map names it Garden for the Garrison, and Juliette Kinzie wrote of its fruit in 1831. A separate field that belonged to the fort is drawn further west on the same map. It is not built here. It is a field, not a building, and belongs with the land and plants.

The print and the copies we checked all show the low part's roof rising less than the tall part's. 25 degrees is our first guess for the low part, about 1.4 meters high over its 2.6 meter wall. The slope and the sizes are not measured from the drawing. The tall roof keeps its 38 degree guess. No real July 1835 slope is claimed.

Who the partners were comes from our notes, from the pair of last names. John H. Kinzie and Lieutenant Hunter came to Chicago together in February 1833. They laid out lots on their land north of the river. Both helped pay for the Lake House in 1835. A book's Kinzie, Hunter and Co., who sold wood, is the same pair. No record gives the firm's full name for the store house. So the men behind it are our guess. Three different Kinzies traded in this town, John, James and Robert. We have buildings for all of them. So who this is matters, and we say so.

An old drawing shows one small chimney above the main roof. So we build one, where before we had two big ones on the wings. That does not prove there was no hidden chimney. Its size, place and that it lasted to July 1835 are our guess.

The light at the mouth of the Chicago River, the first one on Lake Michigan. Samuel Lasby was its first keeper. No record says who kept it on 1 July 1835. Wentworth names William M. Stevens as keeper when he came in October 1836. Nothing we found covers the time between.
The long wall faces back toward the fort. That is where everyone who used it came from. Our guess.

The low part's long front has a door near its far end, and one small window next to the tall part, as in the 1867 drawing. That they were there, and how many, come from the picture. Their places and sizes are our guesses. The main part keeps its own front door.
The highest wall, at the front, is 4 meters. Other parts step down from 1.2 to 3.3 meters. These are our guesses, not measures. The site stays lower than the finished hotel of three floors.

The notice calls it a House, and the June copy of the same notice calls it a dwelling House. That is its known use, and the only one. If anyone lived in it on 1 July 1835 is a different question we do not answer.
The one chimney comes up through the roof, not up the end wall. Where along the roof it sits is our guess from the drawing, still to be checked. Its place and size are not known.
The open ground inside the buildings, for as long as there were buildings round it. It starts with the rebuilt fort. It ends when the main buildings were torn down in the summer of 1856.

We know the men who ran the inn, in order. Archibald Caldwell ran it for James Kinzie by 1829. Then came Elijah Wentworth in 1830, Charles Taylor from 1831 to 1833, and William Walters from 1833 to 1836. We take it that the stable went with the house. No stable hand is named. No record ties any person to this building.

The men who ran it, in order, are known. Archibald Caldwell ran it for James Kinzie by 1829, when he got a license to sell drink. Elijah Wentworth ran it from early 1830. Charles and Mary Taylor ran it from 1831 to 1833. William Walters ran it from 1833 to 1836. So Walters covers 1 July 1835. It is marked as our guess, because the same records also say it stopped being an inn in 1834. A keeper of a closed inn makes no sense, and someone needs to settle it.

The dates start when the log cabin got its front of two floors. That is the shape we build. When that happened is not agreed, even inside one website. One page says that in 1827, Samuel Miller and his brother John, with Archibald Clybourne, added a house of two floors to the cabin, facing the river. Another page says the brothers opened a store about 1829, and made it bigger in 1830 to run it as an inn. We use 1827, because it tells of the change in shape we build. The 1830 page tells of a change of trade. Both may be right: a new part in 1827, and an inn in 1830. Either way it had its 1835 shape well before the day we show. The end is the least we can say, not its fate. No record says when it came down. So the dates end with 1835. Add more when proof appears.

In the picture the doors are raised above the ground. So the lower floor is 3.1 meters tall, and the two upper floors are 2.35 meters each. That keeps the wall at 7.8 meters, with room for the door above its step. These are our guesses, not measures from Gifford.
The picture shows a flag flying. But the picture, made years later with no date, does not show it flew on 1 July 1835. Showing it here, and the way it moves in the breeze, are our guesses.

The doors at ground level in the picture have broad, plain frames. So we add plain frames around the doors, with no fancy top. Their sizes and colors are our guess, not measured. Nothing else about the building changes.

In the picture, the boards of the wall go on up into the pointed end above the roof edge. They are wall, not roof. Both pointed ends are built this way. The far end is our guess, since no picture shows it. Nothing else about the building changes.

The plan names it Wash house. Hubbard says the men and women of the fort did their washing in one. That is the only record of what anyone did in any building on the fort's outer ground. It is why we know what this building was for, though we know none of its sizes.

The plan names it Wash house on the fort's outer ground. Hubbard says the men and women of the fort did their washing in it. So whose it was is in his words. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the fort's work buildings were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

The room for the fort's guards, at the south gate. Part of it burned in the fire of September 1827. That fire burned the soldiers' rooms and the store house. John Kinzie's son got up on the roof with a wet blanket and saved it. That is the most lively thing anyone wrote about the inside of this fort.

The fort's trading shop, where soldiers bought what their food and supplies did not cover. Who ran it on 1 July 1835 is not known. A book says the brother of John Kinzie's wife worked as the fort's trader about 1830. That is five years too early, and a different question.
The pointed cap rises 0.45 meters above the box. Its slope and how it is built are our guess. The plan's label tells nothing more.

The roof now has a slope of 30 degrees, our guess, not the 38 degrees we had before. When we first checked it against the print, the roof top was much too high. This is a fix to match the picture. The building's size and wall height stay the same. It is not a measured slope. The print has no date.

The same dates and the same one person as the first mound. Juliette Kinzie saw it in 1831, and no one else ever did. It starts with the fort and ends when the soldiers left for good. These dates are not new proof. They come from the same sentence as the first mound.
The second saw man's home: a shack of boards. That is what the poorest builders lived in.

The record calls it James Kinzie's home, and that is all it says about its use. If anyone lived in it on 1 July 1835 is a different question. We do not answer it. James Kinzie built the Green Tree inn at Lake and Canal in 1833. He traded and built all over the west side in these years. No record puts him under this roof in the summer of 1835. So we place no people in it, rather than guess.

The record calls it a store building, the first on Lake Street. A warning goes with every known fact here. The claim is in a note with no author, added at the foot of a page of maps on a website. Our own notes call it the weakest text in that set, never to rank above Andreas. We use it because it is plain, and the only place this building is found, not because it is strong.
The records do not agree. The Wolf Point story says 1828. The list of hotels says it opened in 1823.

The south one of the two piers that hold open the 1834 cut through the sand bar. It was the first of the works started. The harbor work began on the south side of the river in June 1833, under Major George Bender, who led Fort Dearborn, with Henry Handy to help. The north pier was built out as far in the spring of 1834. This pier was always the shorter one. The sand drifts south along this shore. So the north pier takes the sand, and this one holds the other side of the channel.

The street is in the land records. This building is not. Its front is set one meter past the edge of the drawn street. It is laid out by our plan for the west side, with gaps between and work ground behind. Its place is our guess, and it claims no known lot or address.

In the 1867 print, the tall Miller House has logs on its lower floor and boards running up and down on its upper floor and pointed end. We used to give it long boards on both floors. We use the picture now. But the picture was made years later. It does not prove how the house looked on 1 July 1835. The house is still 5.2 meters to the roof edge. Where the logs stop and the boards start, at 2.6 meters, is our guess. So are the board sizes. The low part, the front openings and the two roofs follow the picture too. The lines between the boards were first too faint to see, so we made them wider. They are a drawing trick, not a measure of old boards.

The tall front keeps its six openings: below, a window, a door and a window, and above, three windows. Their number and order come from the 1867 print, made years later and set in 1833. All their sizes and places are our guesses. No exact spot where the artist stood, and no July 1835 look, is known.
The town bakery. It was on Lake Street, with the inns and stores. It made bread for the people who stayed there.

Its use comes from the meat plant. The plant's own record says the barrel and salting space is outside its walls. A book tells what was packed here, but not where. No one is placed in it. That would be a person, and this record claims only a building.

Its use comes from a picture and from the place. A picture the owner gave us on 18 August 2026 draws low store houses on the banks below the drawbridge. This stretch is where the river traffic and the town's only bridge over the main river met in July 1835. The goods, the trade and who ran it are not guessed. That would be a person, and this record claims a building.

Its use comes from a picture and from the place. A picture the owner gave us on 18 August 2026 draws low store houses on the banks below the drawbridge. This stretch is where the river traffic, the town's only bridge over the main river, and the road to the fort all met in July 1835. The goods, the trade and who ran it are not guessed. That would be a person, and this record claims a building.
In Cameron's picture the window is about half as tall as the door. Its height follows from our guess for the door. It is a guess, not a measure.

The north pier of the country's harbor work. It is the north one of two piers that hold open the 1834 cut through the sand bar. It keeps the drifting sand out and the channel clear. It is the reason there is a harbor at Chicago at all. Before it, the river turned south behind the sand bar. Ships stopped half a mile out, and small boats carried their goods in. Congress gave $25,000 for the work in March 1833. The schooner Illinois came through the cut on 12 July 1834, the first ship into the river. In 1835 Congress gave $32,800 more. By the day we show, Chicago is the busiest port in the West, and this pier is why.
The 1902 picture shows boards that run side to side. So our wood house gets long boards that lap over each other.
It is one of the first made-up roofs that fill the town for July 1835. Nothing proves this building stood.

A picture from 1842 shows three small dark windows in the tower. Two are clear, and one is not. Their sizes and places are our guess, not measured. Each is a plain hole with no frame. No door can be seen at the bottom.

Three records. A book says Hogan used a log house as a store. It also says a small log building near the corner of Lake and South Water. Currey says a log building about where South Water meets Lake. No record tells how the corners or gaps were done, or if it had boards on it. We build squared logs, the most common kind here in 1835. All three records say logs.

Two levels, as a photo from 1855 shows: an open lower level on posts, and a walkway at the second floor. Using that for July 1835 is our choice. We do not know when it was built. The wall height stays the same. The exact floor, rail and posts are our guess.
Two windows and then the door on the long front, in Gale's picture. Andreas shows a different side. The number is from the picture. The spacing is our guess.
It is a choice for the kind, not proof about this building.
A choice for this kind of older log cabin, from our plans. It is not proof about this building.
It is a choice for the kind, not proof about this building.
A choice for this kind of deep wood cottage, from our plans. It is not proof about this building.
This is a choice we made for this kind of building. It is not a record of this building.
It is a choice for the kind, not proof about this building.
Not known. The book's word worn is about the flag, not the pole. We leave the pole bare, not whitewashed, since nothing says either.

Not known. The book gives the pole's height and nothing else: not what it was made of, its color or its steps. We build it as a trimmed round log, the same color as the town's log buildings. A flagpole at a fort on the frontier was a tree. A white pole would look very different over the fence, and nothing backs one.

Not known at this fort. The 1803 order tells of blockhouses that guard the walls from both floors, with holes to shoot through. So shooting holes are what the building is for. But that order was for the first fort. The pattern, spacing and height of every slot here are ours.
Not known at this fort. The upper floor sticking out over the lower is the main thing about a blockhouse. We built it at a usual size. When you look at it, you see what a blockhouse is, not proof.

Not known in words. A pointed roof with four sides over a near-square plan is the usual kind. A list from 1808 for the first fort says the blockhouses did not yet have their cupolas. That is about the first fort, not this one. The cupola we build now is read from pictures of this fort. It is kept as its own item, with its own confidence.
Not known. The slope is lower than the long buildings, because a pointed roof over a wide plan gets tall fast.
Not known. A roof with one slope, leaning on the wall, is what a gun shed is. A two-sided roof would be just as much a guess.
No record says. It is bare stone. But many early towers like this were painted white. Nothing says which this was. A white tower would look quite different from across the river.
Not known. A roof of two slopes, not the cone of the 1803 order, for the reason in the note on how it was built. Either way it is our choice.
Not known. How far each part of the fence steps out from the line, which makes the zigzag. Three feet was usual.
Not known. Logs, like the fort's other wood buildings. But nothing backs it for this one.

Not known. The 1830 plan draws the corners as small boxes sticking out. This is that shape, at a size the plan allows. It could be off by two fifths, more than the rest, since the corners are small on the map.
Not known. A mound of earth with a flat top and a wood door in one end.
Not known. How high the mound stands above the ground.
No record says. The tower has a walkway and a glass room for the light at the top, not a roof. The cap over the light is our usual one.
Our guess. Bare boards, our usual, and how every work building on the river here is done.
Our guess. Bare boards, our usual, and how every work building on the river here is done. Paint on a packing house would be the bigger claim.
Our guess. Bare boards, our usual. Two of the pictures the owner gave us show it on work buildings by the river. Paint on a freight shed would be the bigger claim.
Boards with no paint. Made up.

Two wide bases under the lifting frames. The 1884 picture shows wide bases under the tall frames, not many small boxes. At first we built them as solid boxes of logs. Looking closer at the whole picture, it shows a board top over a row of upright posts driven down. So each base is now a platform about 3.6 by 6 meters, on posts set close together, with a board top. The sizes, the posts and how deep they go are our guess, not from the drawing. Nothing solid fills them. We do not claim a match yet.

A fit to how it looks, not a measure. We matched the roof's peak to Gifford's picture. Our old 38 degree roof came out too high. About 31 and a half degrees fits, so we use 32. It is not a measured slope.

Three people wrote about these houses. Wau-Bun calls them a group of log buildings. Andreas calls them small log buildings. McKee, who built houses here in 1823, said they were all made of logs. Logs are the one thing all three agree on.
Wau-Bun says named people lived in the cabins, and later calls the group these homes. They were homes.

Wau-Bun counts them loosely, two or three, and that looseness is the record. So we keep the book's words, not a number. One cabin is built. We build a building, not a group. Picking two or three would make up the number the book would not give, and their spacing. So the model shows less than was there. You see one cabin where there were at least two, and this note says so.

Wau-Bun says it had an odd-shaped roof. We build five roofs side by side. There is a big middle roof, two smaller wing roofs and two narrow back roofs. An old drawing shows the big front roof and a smaller side roof. It can't show the back or where the roofs meet, so all of that is our guess.

Wau-Bun says the buildings near the Agency House were log homes for the government's workers, the blacksmith among them. Andreas says the same of 1830, naming McKee. McKee himself said all the houses there were logs. But those writers tell of the blacksmith's home. That his shop was logs too is our guess. Logs are the only kind of wall anyone saw here then.

Wau-Bun names the job, not the building. It says log houses around the Agency House were homes for the government's workers: the blacksmith, the striker and the laborers. So the striker had a home. That it was its own house, not a room in the blacksmith's, is our guess. So we trust it less than the other two houses here.

Wau-Bun says it had a middle part, two wings and two back parts, the same on both sides from the front. We build that shape. The sizes and roofs are our guess, from the book's words and an old drawing. The drawing shows a big front roof and a smaller side roof.
Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, says a house just finished by Mark Beaubien.

Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, says a house just finished by Mark Beaubien. It burned down on 4 March 1851. It was renamed the Chicago Hotel in 1838. A theater company used the dining room in 1837. Those changed its use, not its shape, so they do not start a new stage.
Wau-Bun calls it a showy white building of two floors, with bright blue wood shutters. White paint was itself special at Wolf Point in 1831. The book tells of it because the building stood out.
Wau-Bun calls it a showy white building of two floors.

Wau-Bun calls it a solid, compact little building of logs, cut and squared. McKee, who came in 1823, said all the houses there were logs. He said the agency house later got boards part way up its walls. Cut and squared logs is just what we build. The boards are kept in a separate note, since how far up they went, and when, are not known.
A place to keep the soldiers' roots and food for the winter. It is dug into the bank of the river.

The four chimneys are placed to match the picture, as best we can. Their heights above the roof are 1.75, 0.6, 1 and 1.2 meters. Their sizes and caps are our guess, not measured. The picture shows that they were there, and roughly how they looked.

No supports in the water is the smallest guess. Our builder allows it: a short crossing goes end to end with nothing in the water. Without a number, it would stand two supports in a six meter stream. The river bridges needed two supports each over 56 and 72 meters. Twelve meters of log needs none.
